title: Rennie reveals thinking behind Cortez Ratima selection over Cameron Roigard
article_text:
All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie has said his selection of Chiefs halfback Cortez Ratima over Cameron Roigard comes down to wanting Ratima to “have a crack” against England this weekend at Allianz Stadium.

Ratima started for the All Blacks against Wales two weeks ago and came off the bench in last weekend’s 37-12 defeat to England, before getting the nod for their final Test match of 2026.

The All Blacks are on the back of two straight defeats on their end-of-year Northern Tour, the last of which was their largest defeat in history against a team from the Northern Hemisphere.

Rennie has made six changes to his starting lineup for the Nations Championship rematch against Steve Borthwick’s England at Twickenham on Saturday evening local time.

Ratima will partner Richie Mo’unga, whose inclusion in the starting lineup has shifted Damian McKenzie to fullback.

The All Blacks head coach, who said the players have responded well during training, explained why the Chiefs halfback got the nod over Roigard.

“Oh, Cam’s had a great year, and he’s started just about every test, but we’re really happy with how Cortez has gone,” Rennie told reporters at their team naming press conference in London.

“We thought he [Ratima] had a strong game against Wales and off the bench last week, and so we are keen for him to have a crack.

“And like I say, bringing Cam’s experience on late in the game, we think it will work for us.”

And while the All Blacks have enjoyed strong moments during this Nations Championship end-of-year tour, against England, their attack stalled.

For large periods, they were unable to break the resolute England defence, constantly looking out of sorts in possession.

When they looked to kick and relieve pressure, Roigard and McKenzie did so inaccurately, gifting possession back to England, which frustrated Rennie.

“Oh, it was pretty simple; we kicked poorly. I think like Cam’s been excellent, kicked really well in the Australian series.

“But I think one of them [against England], he was under a little bit of pressure; the rest he wasn’t, and likewise, Damian put one up to apply a little bit of pressure, and it was too deep as well.

“So, if we’re going to kick, you either want to find grass or you kick somewhere where we can apply a bit of pressure, and so I think we kicked six times contestable. Only one of them we’re able to compete with.

Borthwick has made five changes to his 23-man squad for the All Blacks rematch, but Rennie isn’t reading too much into it.

“I guess tactically they’re trying to make sure they’ve got plenty of energy. They’re also heading into a Six Nations in about six weeks or so, I guess their season’s just starting and haven’t made massive change, but rotated a few.

“And everyone they’re talking about has played a fair bit of footy in the jersey as well, so that’s a good English side. I think in some of those spots, it’s very tight who starts and who doesn’t. We’re not reading too much into it.”

title: Two teams face Nations Championship relegation under 2030 playoff plans
article_text:
Two teams could be relegated from the Nations Championship from 2030 under controversial plans being developed by the tournament organisers.

The Guardian has learned that the favoured mechanism for introducing relegation is for the bottom sides in the northern and southern hemisphere tables to face a one-legged playoff match against the winners of the equivalent tables in the tier-two Nations Cup, which is run by World Rugby. The tier one sides would be guaranteed home advantage in the tie, which based on this year’s inaugural competition would see matches between Italy and Georgia and Fiji and the USA, with the winner of each securing a place in the Nations Championship two years later.

The introduction of two relegation playoffs would see an extra match added to the final series, the first of which begins on Friday at the Allianz Stadium, with the bottom-ranked sides Italy and Fiji opening proceedings before the third v third game between Ireland and Australia.

From 2030 there would be seven playoff games, with the top five sides in each hemisphere meeting each other in addition to the two relegation playoffs. As the Guardian reported earlier this month there is pushback from some unions about introducing relegation, particularly those in Italy and Wales, which may increase if it is confirmed that two sides can be demoted.

Abi Tierney, the Welsh Rugby Union chief executive, said recently it would be “cataclysmic” were Wales relegated and there have been suggestions that the 10 founding unions of the Nations Championship, which does not include invited guests Fiji and Japan, may seek to ensure they are exempt.

World Rugby, however, is adamant that the Nations Championship was only sanctioned on the basis of an open system of promotion and relegation being introduced and will resist any attempt to protect the biggest unions.

Its creation was narrowly approved at a vote of the World Rugby Council in Paris before the 2023 World Cup final on the proviso that it would be an open league from 2030, with sources present at the meeting telling the Guardian that moves to ringfence the 10 founding members would need to go to the council for approval, and could be denied.

The original vote required a 75% majority to pass and the motion received 41 votes for and 10 against, meaning it won a majority of 80%, so reopening the debate would be a risky move as it could throw the tournament into turmoil.

The Rugby Football Union chief executive, Bill Sweeney, declined to go into details when asked how relegation would be introduced earlier this month.

“There’s a review group that has been set up by World Rugby and is chaired by [World Rugby chair] Brett Robinson,” Sweeney said. “They’re looking at how the aspect of promotion and relegation can be set up. The basic premise is still the same, how that comes into effect needs to be sorted out.”

In addition to determining the relegation mechanism, the Nations Championship, which is a joint venture between the 10 Six Nations and Sanzaar unions, also have to agree financial protections for unions who suffered relegation.

A parachute payment system similar to that offered by the Premier League is likely to be introduced, but many of the bigger unions reject claims that relegation would prove existential, pointing out that those going down would not lose their place in the Six Nations or Rugby Championship.A number of unions are also increasingly convinced that introducing two relegation playoffs would add to the commercial value of the competition, creating two blockbuster ties that would generate large ticket sales and television audiences.

Selling tickets for the inaugural final series has been challenging after three successive weekends of England games at Twickenham, particularly for the opening night tonighton Friday, when the stadium’s upper tier will be closed and tens of thousands of empty seats are expected.

title: Former England scrum-half and commentator Nigel Starmer-Smith dies at 81
article_text:
Former England scrum-half and broadcaster Nigel Starmer-Smith has died at the age of 81, his family has announced.

Starmer-Smith played for Harlequins and the Barbarians, and made seven appearances for England between 1969 and 1971.

After retiring from the sport, Starmer-Smith moved into media and presented the BBC’s weekly highlights programme Rugby Special for 15 years. He was diagnosed with dementia in 2015.

Starmer-Smith’s son Charlie posted on social media: “Dad passed away peacefully this morning after a long battle with dementia.

“He was [as they say in rugby circles] one of life’s great tourists. A rugby player, commentator, editor, writer, raconteur, charity fundraiser, volunteer, speaker, prankster, family man, life and soul of the party but, above all, the greatest father anyone could wish to have.

“He did everything for us and, despite having to bury two of his children at cruelly young ages, both he and my mum refused to let the cavernous holes that Charlotte and Julian left behind define them. Just as I choose not to let the cruel condition that robbed him of his ability to communicate [and ultimately of his dignity] define my memories of him.

“He was a modest man and he’d hate for people to make a fuss. He loved to laugh but not as much as he loved to see others laughing. So for those that knew him think of a happy memory and smile. For that’s how I’ll remember him.”

title: New Zealand’s players not subjected to anti-doping testing during tour of South Africa
article_text:
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

New Zealand’s players were not subjected to any anti-doping testing during their Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour, raising questions over South Africa’s procedures after a drop in the number of tests conducted within the country.

The All Blacks took on the Springboks in three international matches on South African soil in August and September, and also faced the nation’s four United Rugby Championship (URC) franchises on tour.

A figure familiar with the tour agreement outlined to The Independent that responsibility for testing during the tour lay with the South African Institute for Drug-Free Sports (Saids), an organisation that has recorded a drop in the number of tests across sport in recent years.

Data published by Saids earlier this year revealed that just 225 total tests were conducted within rugby union by the organisation in the calendar year up to 31 March 2026 – more than in the equivalent 12 months prior (166) but significantly fewer than a decade earlier (753). The equivalent number of tests conducted by UK Anti-Doping (Ukad) rose from 998 to 1,241 over that same period.

Within sport as a whole, Saids’ total number of tests has fallen from 2324 in 2023/24 to 1664 in 2025/26. In March 2024, Africa’s only anti-doping laboratory accredited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) in Bloemfontein was suspended, forcing Saids to send samples to be tested overseas – the lab has had that accreditation fully revoked.

Three South African rugby players, including four-cap Springbok Asenathi Ntlabakanye, were found to have committed anti-doping rule violation in the 2025/26 period outlined. Prop Ntlabakanye is serving an 18-month ban after testing positive for hormone and metabolic modulator Anastrozole – though a panel found his violation was “not intentional”.

Sources within multiple Test-playing environments have expressed surprise at the lack of testing during the landmark series, describing it as highly unusual. The Springboks came from behind to win 3-1, with the fourth and final encounter between the two rivals held in the United States in Baltimore.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on the part of either of the two teams involved, or the URC franchises involved in the inaugural Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour.

All players could have been subject to no-notice testing via World Rugby’s testing programme, as is the case throughout the year. Those based outside of South Africa would also be subject to testing as part of the National Anti-Doping Agency testing pool for the country in which they play their domestic rugby.

“World Rugby operates a risk-based no-notice anti-doping programme in line with the World Anti-Doping Agency Code,” a World Rugby spokesperson said. “All qualified Men’s and Women’s Rugby World Cup team players are included within a dedicated out of competition testing pool which is not competition specific.

“This means that all these players are subject to testing on a no-notice, any location basis throughout the calendar year, including within international competition windows. This means that over the course of the year, both teams are tested in and out of competition in line with World Rugby’s programme and are also subject to testing undertaken by the respective National Anti-Doping Agencies at both the international and domestic/cross border club levels.”

South Africa Rugby (SA Rugby) and Saids have been contacted for comment. New Zealand Rugby declined to comment, though confirmed that their players had not been tested during the course of the seven-week tour.

title: Rennie rolls the dice at halfback as All Blacks name new captain for England
article_text:
All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie has been forced to make several changes to his last Test team of 2026, making six adjustments to the starting side that faced England last weekend at Allianz Stadium.

The All Blacks will look to bounce back after back-to-back losses to Northern Hemisphere sides as they take on England this weekend, again, in the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend.

World Rugby Men’s 15s Player of the Year nominee Jordie Barrett will captain the All Blacks for the very first time, with Codie Taylor ruled out through injury. Taylor picked up a calf injury in the first ten minutes of last week’s defeat, and won’t feature in the final Test match of 2026.

The big selection calls come in the No.9 and No.10 jerseys, with Rennie opting to bench Cameron Roigard for Chiefs halfback Cortez Ratima. The halfback has featured predominantly off the bench when fit on this end-of-year Northern Tour, and will partner Crusaders first-five Richie Mo’unga.

Mo’unga’s place at first-five shifts Damian McKenzie back to fullback, while 94-Test veteran Rieko Ioane and Leicester Fainga’anuku come into the starting lineup.

Fainga’anuku will partner Barrett in midfield, while Ioane will start on the right wing with Josh Moorby on his favoured left wing.

In the forwards, Asafo Aumua starts at hooker alongside Ethan de Groot and Fletcher Newell in the front row.

The second row of Fabian Holland and Scott Barrett is retained, as are Peter Lakai and Wallace Sititi in the loose-forwards. It’s a second Test start for Blues loose-forward Anton Segner, who is promoted from the bench to the starting No.6 role.

There are new faces on the bench, including Xavier Numia, George Bell, Josh Lord, Ethan Blackadder, and Timoci Tavatavanawai. Beauden Barrett and Roigard make up the backline reserves.

Rennie said the squad have been honest in their review of last week’s defeat, and will need to improve on all aspects of the game if they are to earn a victory in the final Nations Championship Test of the season.

“Last weekend hurt. We own that performance. We’ve been really honest with ourselves about where we fell short, and now we have an awesome opportunity to go again against a quality England side. We know how good we’ll need to be on Saturday, and we’re preparing accordingly.

“Huge congratulations to Jordie on being named Captain. He’s been a key part of our leadership group for a long time and is highly respected by his teammates, on and off-field. It’s a massively proud moment for him and the Barrett whanau.

“We want to put in a performance that reflects the work this group has done all year, and that shows our fans how much we appreciate their support.”

Unavailable for selection due to injury: Will Jordan; Codie Taylor; Tupou Vaa’i; Anton Lienert-Brown.

title: Woolly hats, battered bodies and big TV numbers mark rugby union’s new festival finale
article_text:
It would be a stretch to describe the Nations Championship finals weekend as the “Glastonbury of Rugby” quite yet. Cher will certainly need to wrap up warm if she is planning to make a cameo appearance; with forecast temperatures of 3C, plenty more thermal vests and woolly hats will be in evidence than at Worthy Farm in June.

There will also be significant gaps in the Allianz Stadium moshpit when Italy and Fiji and Ireland and Australia kick off the three-day finals extravaganza beneath the Friday night lights. Even the organisers concede that Friday has been “a challenge” in terms of ticket sales and that’s without factoring in rush-hour traffic and public transport disruption.

But, whisper it, Test rugby’s newest vehicle has been appealing to viewers sitting comfortably at home. The organisers say the tournament is set to attract a total broadcast audience in excess of 100 million people, comparable to the 118 million fans in core markets who tuned in to this year’s Six Nations. The Nations Championship will clearly have spanned many more games – 42 compared to 15 – but the hope is that ITV will have seen enough to renew for future tournaments.

Stadium attendances are also said to be up by 4% compared to previous November international windows, although punchy ticket prices this weekend seem to have deterred plenty with Christmas around the corner. The stadium will not be filled to capacity on either Saturday or Sunday and, as Andy Farrell, Ireland’s head coach points out, it is not as simple as scheduling a game and expecting tens of thousands of green-shirted fans to drop everything. “Nobody knew until last weekend when we’d be playing,” said Farrell. “The Irish can’t buy flights over here because they’re £1,000 so that doesn’t work really.”

There is also the small matter of player welfare; on top of the summer travel travails of some northern teams can now be added some visibly shattered southern bodies. “I can only imagine how the southern hemisphere boys are feeling now at the back end of their season,” agrees Scotland’s captain Sione Tuipulotu, himself now sidelined with a minor knee problem.

On the flipside, Tuipulotu and others have enjoyed the amended format in other ways. Scotland, for example, have been to South Africa and Argentina and hosted New Zealand and Australia inside five months. “I’ve loved it,” says Tuipulotu, who should be back fit early next month. “Scottish teams don’t normally get those summer fixtures.”

Even New Zealand’s Dave Rennie, whose side are crawling to the end of a year in which they will have played 13 of their 17 games (including provincial tour matches in South Africa) away from home, likes the change. “I like the concept. The interesting thing is you’ve got the northern hemisphere teams coming down to us at the end of their year and vice versa when we come up here. I just think our [Nations Championship] year is a little bit different to what it will be in two years’ time when it is on again.”

England’s Steve Borthwick, for his part, is also upbeat ahead of this weekend’s rematch with the All Blacks. “There’s jeopardy in it, you start thinking about things which you weren’t thinking of previously in the autumn. I would suggest that is a real positive aspect.” Farrell, meanwhile, shares Rennie’s view that 2028 should be less stressful for all involved. “This is a little bit different because the World Cup is next year. People are always going to have one eye on that. I think everyone’s still trying to figure it out but it’s certainly interesting. Let’s see how this weekend goes.”

South Africa’s captain, Siya Kolisi, always someone with an eye on the bigger picture, is another fan regardless of whether his team edge out France in Sunday’s grand final. “I think it’s giving [the November Tests] more drive and more fans are excited about it. We’ve enjoyed it certainly as a team and I’m sure the other guys have all enjoyed it. Hopefully it continues.”

More attention-grabbing games this weekend would further cement the concept.

The venue for the 2028 edition will not be confirmed until the spring and it would not be a big surprise if Paris or other French cities emerge as strong contenders. There remains a vision, too, for future promotion/relegation playoffs for each hemisphere; not every union fancies it but to allow the world’s top dozen sides to remain unchallenged for ever would be a catastrophic look for the game’s global profile.

That is not to say aspects of future editions cannot be finessed. The north-south trophy for the winning hemisphere was on precisely nobody’s lips on Wednesday evening when all the head coaches – bar South Africa – were all speaking simultaneously in the Spirit of Rugby suite in Twickenham, temporarily transformed into an oval-shaped Tower of Babel. A Glastonbury festival vibe deep in a European winter might also be more practicable over a two-day weekend, or at least at a venue where large numbers of fans can party inside in the warm.

This weekend, regardless, already means different things to different people. Kolisi, as you would expect, is purely focused on winning yet another trophy for South Africa. “Everything that happened before that final game doesn’t matter. It’s all about whether you can rock up on the day and play to the best of your ability. And that’s what we want to do.”

title: 'It does feel crazy': Blitzboks eyeing major side quests as new SVNS starts
article_text:
The road to the 2028 Olympic Games starts in Dubai this weekend, but Blitzboks captain Siviwe Soyizwapi insists South Africa will not be distracted by what lies at the end of it.

The 2027 HSBC SVNS Series doubles as the first major step towards qualification for Los Angeles, with four automatic Olympic berths on offer across the campaign. For a South African team arriving as reigning SVNS Series and World Championship winners, expectations are naturally high.

Yet as the Blitzboks prepare to open their season against Australia, Argentina and the USA in Pool A, Soyizwapi says thoughts of Olympic qualification are being parked in favour of a narrower focus.

“When you start an Olympic cycle, it just adds a bit of pressure if you focus on it, so our goal is to just to kind of acknowledge that it is a significant season with Olympic qualification on the line, but rather focus on what is in front of us,” said Soyizwapi.

“The focus will be on our processes, and we will approach and attack every tournament separately.”

Instead, the veteran skipper wants South Africa’s attention fixed firmly on building momentum from the first event of the season.

“For this weekend, it always gets us excited to kick things off and you want to start well. We will be looking for that to get momentum going into Cape Town and the rest of the season.”

Soyizwapi, set to captain the Blitzboks for the 38th time, admitted it had been difficult to comprehend how quickly the off-season had disappeared.

“It does feel crazy that we are at the start of yet another season – it feels like yesterday when we finished off the previous one in France in May.

“The days and weeks have gone so quickly back in Stellenbosch, and here we are, back in Dubai, ready to kick things off again, hopefully with a bang, leading to a great season.”

Dubai has traditionally been fertile ground for South Africa and Soyizwapi believes the tournament’s place on the calendar has often worked in their favour.

“This has always been a successful venue and a good tournament for us, mostly I think because we are coming off a hard preseason.

“We also had tough conditioning and games in the build-up. It is always exciting to start off the season here, we have lots of support and love playing here.”

Among those eager for a strong opening is Ricardo Duarttee, whose breakout Dubai performances in 2023 helped launch his international sevens career.

“Yes, we were disappointed with not getting the same results in 2024 and 2025, but we arrived here knowing that we worked hard and will play as a team,” said Duarttee.

“We have a clear vision of what we want to achieve and if we stick to our system, we will be a tough team to beat.”

title: Former England scrum-half and commentator Starmer-Smith dies aged 81
article_text:
Former England scrum-half and rugby union commentator Nigel Starmer-Smith has died aged 81.

He had been diagnosed with dementia in 2015.

Starmer-Smith represented Harlequins and the Barbarians, and made seven appearances for England between 1969-71.

After his retirement in 1976, Starmer-Smith moved into broadcasting and journalism.

He voiced the BBC's highlights programme Rugby Special for 15 years and commentated for ITV at the 2003 World Cup in Australia, won by England.

Starmer-Smith's son Charlie spoke about his father's condition in 2021, saying dementia was a "big issue" in sport and describing how the family were only able to see him through the window during the Covid-19 pandemic.

He said that getting knocked out in a game of rugby was "like a badge of honour" during his father's playing days but also said dementia ran in their family, with his uncle also dying from the disease.

"Dad passed away peacefully this morning after a long battle with dementia," Charlie posted on social media on Thursday.

"He was (as they say in rugby circles) one of life's great tourists. A rugby player, commentator, editor, writer, raconteur, charity fundraiser, volunteer, speaker, prankster, family man, life and soul of the party, but, above all, the greatest father anyone could wish to have.

"He did everything for us and, despite having to bury two of his children at cruelly young ages, both he and my Mum refused to let the cavernous holes that Charlotte and Julian left behind define them.

"Just as I choose not to let the cruel condition that robbed him of his ability to communicate (and ultimately of his dignity), define my memories of him.

"He was a modest man and he'd hate for people to make a fuss. He loved to laugh but not as much as he loved to see others laughing. So for those that knew him think of a happy memory and smile. For that's how I'll remember him."

The BBC paid tribute to Starmer-Smith, with head of sport, Philip Bernie, saying: Nigel was a very distinguished commentator for the BBC after his successful rugby playing days.

"His enthusiasm and love for the game always shone through in his excellent, engaging broadcasting across so many great matches he memorably called, and for Rugby Special.

"All our thoughts and sympathies are with his family and those closest to him."

title: Sione Tuipulotu hopeful of rapid Glasgow Warriors return after Scotland injury blow
article_text:
Scotland captain Sione Tuipulotu is hopeful of making his return before the end of the year after receiving good news on his knee injury.

The Glasgow Warriors centre suffered a ligament strain against New Zealand earlier this month and subsequently missed the wins over Australia and Japan.

But the 29-year-old said he's feeling grateful after scans in London revealed the ligament issue is not as serious as first feared.

Speaking at the media launch of the Nations Championship finals weekend at Allianz Stadium in London, he said: "I got the good news, obviously, that it wasn’t like a serious injury or anything like that.

"I was a little bit worried, to be honest, just because whenever you get sent down to a specialist, you start to be like, ‘Why am I getting sent down to someone important?’

“But it was just good reassuring news from the specialist that this will only be no longer than a month type thing, from when I injured it."

Tuipulotu admitted he knew straight away that something wasn't right after picking up the injury at the end of the defeat to New Zealand on November 7 but was determined to push through in a bid to face the Wallabies.

The Melbourne-raised centre said: "I trained all week. I did both sessions but then when I got to captain’s run, I just felt like something wasn’t right, so I flagged it to the physios and we got the scan.

"I really wanted to play the Australia game, but at this point I’m probably just glad that we ended up getting the scan and figuring out what was wrong.

"I probably would have hurt it if I’d gone out there, so we did the right thing."

While Tuipulotu is with the team in London, he assured the assembled media that there is no chance of a surprise return as Scotland face Argentina on Sunday.

While reluctant to put any definitive timescales on his return, Tuipulotu suggested Glasgow's Champions Cup meeting with Pau on December 11 could be the game he makes his return.

"It’s definitely realistic," he said when asked about the prospect of facing the Top 14 side.

"I was even thinking that I could possibly get back for this week because I feel like in the past, my body’s done well with healing, and I back myself to heal fast, but I don’t want to put a timeline on anything.

"When I’m right to go, I’ll be back. But Pau is definitely a realistic target.”

That means the Scotland skipper will almost certainly be available for the 1872 Cup matches, and the prospect of a head-to-head with his younger brother Mosese.

But that is not a prospect the centre is thrilled with.

"I look forward to the 1872 Cup but I don’t look forward to playing my brother," he said.

In the meantime, Tuipulotu can only watch from the sidelines and offer his words of wisdom to the Scotland side as they look to sign off the year with a third Nations Championship win in a row.

But he's the first to admit he's a frustrated spectator.

“I’ve been at home a lot as well. I’ve got two young boys now, so I’ve just been trying to use my energy there.

“You’re angry about being hurt, but then when you look back at the last, I suppose, two years I’ve had, I haven’t missed a game from injury since my pec [before the 2025 Six Nations], which is a long time ago.

"I’ve got to take it as it comes, and I’ll be fresh and eager to contribute when I get back.”

title: Rassie Erasmus could face even longer ban from World Rugby
article_text:
Rassie Erasmus could be hit with an even longer suspension after reportedly finding himself at the centre of another World Rugby investigation.

The Springboks head coach is already serving a six-match ban, but his punishment could now be extended.

According to the Irish Examiner, both Erasmus and assistant coach Mzwandile Stick are facing separate investigations into their conduct surrounding South Africa’s Nations Championship defeat to Ireland in Dublin last week.

Erasmus is already serving a six-match ban imposed following his criticism of refereeing decisions.

The punishment meant he had to watch the Ireland clash from his hotel room rather than take his place in the coaching box.

However, his behaviour during the match has now attracted further attention.

World Rugby are understood to be investigating a possible breach of his suspension after Erasmus was seen on camera appearing to speak to someone over the telephone.

His microphone was muted throughout the first half, when Ireland established a 17-10 lead. Despite this, Erasmus appeared to be talking while wearing earbuds.

He was also spotted covering his mouth on several occasions and reaching for his phone, prompting questions about whether he was communicating with someone involved in the match.

Of course, there is no evidence that he was speaking to members of the Springboks coaching staff or players. He could have been talking to anyone.

World Rugby are reportedly keen to establish the identity of the person on the other end of the call and whether the interaction breached the conditions of his suspension.

Those conditions prohibit Erasmus from having direct or indirect contact with Springboks players or team management on matchdays.

Any communication with someone involved in the match could therefore result in further disciplinary action.

Assistant coach Stick is also reportedly under investigation following comments he made about the consistency of rugby's disciplinary process.

Stick questioned the decision to clear Ireland's Sam Prendergast over his controversial hip-drop tackle on Fiji's Peceli Yato.

Speaking to reporters, he suggested the outcome would have been very different if the nationalities involved had been reversed.

"If that was a Fijian player tackling an Irish player with that hip-drop, that player would be in Fiji now," Stick said.

His remarks, reported by RTÉ, raised fresh questions about whether disciplinary decisions are applied consistently across international rugby.

No formal charge or suspension against Stick has been announced.

title: Two teams to be cut as Rugby Europe confirm 2028 restructure
article_text:
Rugby Europe has unveiled a new format for the men’s senior competitions that will take effect in 2028.

The Men’s Rugby Europe Championship will resize back to six teams, played in a single round-robin format. This restructuring means the two teams that finish at the bottom will be automatically relegated after the next edition, which Portugal, Georgia, Spain, Romania, the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland, and Poland will contest. The tournament will begin in February with two groups of four teams (Georgia, Romania, Switzerland, and Belgium in Group A; and Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, and Switzerland in Group B), followed by semi-finals and a final.

This marks a return to a format in place for nearly two decades, discontinued in early 2020 when the Championship expanded to eight teams and introduced a knockout stage. In recent years, Badajoz, Paris, and Madrid have hosted the finals, and now Bucharest will have the honour of holding this finals format one last time.

The sixth-placed team will play a playoff against the winner of the upcoming Men’s Rugby Europe Trophy, with the winner securing a spot in the 2028/2029 edition of Rugby Europe’s senior men’s top flight. As for the Trophy, it will retain the exact same number of teams, six, with the two last-placed sides from the upcoming season being relegated to the Conference, which serves as the third tier of the European rugby structure.

Finally, the Conference will adopt a new model, featuring 10 national teams selected based on specific criteria. As Rugby Europe itself explains: “10 teams will be selected at the end of this season using both the MPC criteria and sporting results. The main rationale is to provide more even matches in better playing conditions, with the possibility for Rugby Europe to shuffle pools at the end of every two-year cycle (…).”

Teams not selected to participate in the Conference from 2028 onwards will move into a new division designated as “Development,” which will ensure more competitive matches aimed at fostering more sustainable development. These changes were implemented to reduce costs for the federations, a measure previously advocated by the “Alliance Four,” a group comprising the rugby unions of Georgia, Portugal, Spain, and Romania.

Regarding qualification for the Men’s 2031 Rugby World Cup, this means that, for now, the top four finishers secure a direct spot in the competition, while the status of the fifth-placed team remains to be determined.

Portugal is currently the champion of the Men’s Rugby Europe Championship, with Poland having moved up to the top division in 2026 after winning the Trophy.

title: 'It is what it is': Andy Farrell did his best to fight Dan Sheehan ban
article_text:
Andy Farrell says he did his best to help Dan Sheehan avoid suspension so he could captain Ireland in Friday’s Nations Championship fifth-placed play-off against Australia.

Sheehan was initially yellow-carded for a croc roll on Marco van Staden in the 72nd minute of Saturday’s statement 20-17 win over world champions South Africa.

The offence was subsequently upgraded to red by the foul play review officer, with Sheehan receiving a two-match suspension to rule him out of the Twickenham clash with the Wallabies.

Nick Timoney replaces Sheehan at number eight, while Jacob Stockdale comes in on the left wing for the ill Mack Hansen in the other change to the starting XV.

“We had word that it was a two-game red card that was recommended and we decided to try and convince people that it was a little bit lower than that,” said head coach Farrell.

After Sheehan was sin-binned, Springbok Van Staden received the same punishment for a dangerous clearout on Tadhg Beirne at the same ruck. His yellow card was also retrospectively changed to red.

Lock Beirne, who will captain Ireland against Australia in Sheehan’s absence, felt both players were unfortunate.

“I didn’t think it was a red card but it probably is on the line,” he said of Sheehan.

“I can imagine if it was someone who did it to him in a game maybe I’d probably be calling for them, I don’t know. It’s one of those.

“I didn’t think either of those yellow cards that were upgraded to red were red personally.

“Even from Marco, I didn’t think it was a red card so I was very surprised to hear that they were both red cards after the game.”

Farrell has been short of options at the base of the scrum this autumn.

Hooker Sheehan impressed after being deployed in the number eight role for the first time at Test level against the Springboks amid injuries to Caelan Doris, Jack Conan and Sean Jansen.

Timoney, who normally operates at flanker, regains the jersey, having worn it in Ireland’s 43-15 victory over Fiji on November 14.

Meanwhile, James McNabney returns to the bench as back-row cover after suffering concussion just minutes into his international debut against Fiji and then sitting out the South Africa match.

“That’s what the squad has to be about really: it has to be able to adapt and move on in a positive manner,” said Farrell.

“We’ve had a few of them of late and that can only stand to us, so it’s a good thing in my opinion.”

Hansen overcame a calf injury to start against South Africa. But, having scored a hat-trick against his native Australia last November, the 28-year-old was left in Ireland after feeling unwell.

“He woke up with all sorts of fever this morning: a ‘one out of 10’ according to him, which is pretty bad because he’s normally upbeat,” said Farrell.

“Well ‘one out of 10’ I thought there’s no way we’re taking him because obviously his immune system and all that.”

Stockdale is yet to feature this month and will make his first Ireland appearance since the 36-20 win over Japan in July.

“He’s been training really well and he deserves his shot,” said Farrell. “He’s really keen to get back going internationally.

“For all the wingers who have not been playing, I think they’ve been pretty impressed with how Mack and Rob (Baloucoune) have gone about their business, so there’s been a lot of learning. He’s a good player, so he gets his chance.”

Prop Sam Illo was unavailable for selection because of a throat infection.

title: Exeter are PWR 'contenders', says new boss Bishop
article_text:
New Exeter head coach Oli Bishop feels his side will be title contenders this season in Premiership Women's Rugby.

Bishop was promoted to lead the Chiefs over the summer after Steve Salvin left to become forwards coach with Wales.

The former Ealing and Wasps coach has spent 13 years coaching in the top flight and takes over an Exeter side that he helped finish third last season before a late 40-38 loss at eventual champions Saracens in the play-off semi-finals.

"The girls are in a good place," he told BBC South West.

"We're not changing huge amounts of things, our DNA is our DNA.

"We've looked to bring in an extra coach, this is the first time Chiefs have had three full-time coaches and I think that's going to make a huge difference to what we can do and the detail we can go to.

"So I would say that we're going to be contenders, but I'm also going to say I think this is probably the most competitive season that we're going to see out there this year."

Exeter have had to wait an extra week to begin their campaign in the nine-team PWR.

They start the season with a tough trip to a Bristol side that ran in eight tries in a 48-21 win at Harlequins last week and have brought players including England star Ellie Kildunne and Wales flanker Bethan Lewis.

Exeter have kept most of the squad that got them to the final four in June as they prepare to return to league action after the autumn's WXV matches.

"A big thing for us is continuity and cohesion," Bishop added.

"We're really happy with the squad and staff that we have and that's why we kept as many as we could at the end of the season.

"So we'll be looking to build, we'll be looking to try and do things slightly differently, but again keep our DNA and keep our identity how we want that to be.

"Me and Steve worked a lot last year on the culture and identity of this place and how we would change things from the previous way it was being run.

"I was 100% on board with that, I've made a couple of tweaks here and there, but they're small changes.

"I'm wanting the girls to go out on the weekend and be brave, take the opportunities that are there and be able to express themselves with a clear understanding of how our DNA influences the way that we play."

title: Ellis Genge to quit English rugby after 2027 Rugby World Cup
article_text:
England prop Ellis Genge could be set to quit English rugby following the 2027 Rugby World Cup, with two French clubs reportedly keen to secure his signature.

The Bristol Bears star has attracted interest from overseas, with the prospect of a lucrative contract in either France or Japan.

Genge, 31, remains a key part of Steve Borthwick's England squad and is expected to play a major role at next year's World Cup in Australia.

However, the tournament could mark the end of his international career.

According to reports from RugbyPass in September, Bordeaux-Bègles and Pau are both interested in signing the British & Irish Lions prop.

Pau's reported interest comes despite the club already securing the services of Bath loosehead Beno Obano for 2027.

There is also interest from Japan, where Genge could potentially land a bumper contract.

The forward signed a new long-term deal with Bristol in September 2024, which is understood to run until the summer of 2028.

However, interested clubs reportedly believe they could strike a deal before his contract expires.

Under the RFU's current selection policy, players based overseas are not eligible to represent England in normal circumstances.

A move abroad after the 2027 World Cup could therefore bring Genge's Test career to a close.

The powerful loosehead will be 32 by the time the tournament kicks off in Australia and 36 when the 2031 World Cup takes place.

He could follow in the footsteps of fellow England internationals Jack Willis and Owen Farrell, who have previously opted to continue their careers in France.

The speculation surrounding Genge's future comes amid reports that Bristol Bears are closing in on a record-breaking £2million deal to sign All Blacks superstar Beauden Barrett.

The New Zealander has reportedly agreed a two-year deal to join the Bears following the 2027 Rugby World Cup, although the transfer has yet to be officially announced.

Landing Barrett would represent a huge statement of intent from Bristol, but it also raises questions about their long-term squad planning.

With Genge among the biggest names on their books, his future could become a major talking point over the next 12 months.

However, there is no suggestion at this stage that Barrett's proposed arrival is directly linked to a potential departure for Genge.

title: 'I'm responsible for winning in the future': How SA Rugby is preparing for life after Rassie
article_text:
Cut off the head of the snake and the body will die, or so the old adage goes. After Rassie Erasmus received a six-match ban, South African rugby has an opportunity to demonstrate its success is not entirely dependent on the brilliance of one man.

Whatever the outcome of this turbulent November, the Springboks will one day have to contemplate a future without their talismanic coach, who is contracted until the end of the 2031 World Cup. His greatest legacy might be to leave behind a system capable of sustaining the success he has engineered.

“Rassie’s responsible for winning today, and I’m responsible for winning in the future,” explains SA Rugby’s general manager of high performance.

Succession planning extends beyond identifying the next generation of Springboks. Physiotherapists, doctors, conditioning specialists, team managers and coaches are being prepared for positions that might only become available several years from now.

Until recently, those working with South Africa’s various national teams operated largely in isolation from their counterparts. Wessels has brought people with similar jobs together, regardless of which team they serve. A solution to a problem encountered by the sevens coaches might now benefit the Junior Springboks or women’s side.

“We don’t necessarily want a revolution one day in the Springbok team,” Wessels says. “We simply want evolution.”

But where does South Africa find its coaches? Wessels’s own career provides some answers. His first assignment was coaching the under-nine Cs at Reddam House primary school in Cape Town, an experience more akin to babysitting than coaching rugby. There he encountered Les Kiss, the current Wallabies head coach, who was then working with the Springboks and ran sessions at the school as a favour to the headmaster.

Some of the best coaches in the country are actually coaching at school level. You really are coaching against really world-class coaches, many of whom have got senior franchise experience.

“I just remember thinking, geez, I’ve never seen someone talk about rugby like this,” Wessels recalls.

After spending time with Kiss in Australia, Wessels applied for a coaching position at Bishops, one of South Africa’s most prestigious rugby schools, but was rejected. He travelled two minutes down the road to Rondebosch Boys’ High, requesting an apprenticeship alongside former Springbok hooker Shaun Povey. Together they coached the under-16 As before graduating to the first XV.

A presentation to schoolmasters brought Wessels into contact with Erasmus, then in charge of the Stormers. Armed with his phone number, Wessels persistently badgered him until he was offered work with Western Province and subsequently the Stormers.

Wessels also coached at the University of Cape Town before joining Jake White’s Brumbies as a defensive consultant. In 2016, aged 33, he became the youngest head coach in Super Rugby history when appointed by the Western Force. He subsequently guided the Melbourne Rebels to their first finals appearance in Super Rugby AU in 2020 before returning to South Africa in 2022.

“Some of the best coaches in the country are actually coaching at [school] level,” Wessels says. “You really are coaching against really world-class coaches, many of whom have got senior franchise experience.”

South Africa’s leading rugby schools, with their specialist coaches, sophisticated conditioning programmes and fiercely contested inter-school fixtures, are effectively a network of rugby academies funded by educational institutions.

SA Rugby is increasingly harnessing that expertise. In 2025, four school coaches, all qualified to World Rugby Level 3, were appointed to the national schools and under-18 structures under the mentorship of Junior Springboks head coach Kevin Foote.

At the time of our conversation, 17 schoolboy coaches were due to spend time with Foote’s staff. School coaches also accompany players to Elite Player Development camps, sharing feedback among colleagues back home.

South Africa’s greatest structural advantage, however, might exist on the next rung of the ladder.

Launched in 2008 and co-founded by former Springbok captain Francois Pienaar, the Varsity Cup initially comprised eight universities before the introduction of the second-tier Varsity Shield in 2011. National television coverage afforded student athletes unprecedented exposure while the tournament became a laboratory for experimental laws.

You can’t keep up the facade of being someone else or having somebody else’s personality under pressure.

Among its 61 Springbok graduates are Eben Etzebeth, Handré Pollard, Malcolm Marx, Ox Nche and Kurt-Lee Arendse. Less celebrated is its significance as a finishing school for coaches.

“The Varsity Cup put me on the radar as a coach,” Stormers head coach John Dobson told the competition’s website in 2021.

Franco Smith won the tournament with the University of the Free State in 2015 and was appointed Cheetahs head coach within a month. He subsequently coached Italy before guiding Glasgow Warriors to the 2024 United Rugby Championship title.

Together with community club competitions, the SA Cup and Currie Cup, the tournament allows coaches to hone their craft in progressively more demanding environments before taking charge of professional teams.

But the existence of a ladder does not guarantee that everyone is permitted to climb it.

Jonathan Mokuena, a former Springbok sevens captain who guided North-West University to their maiden Varsity Cup title in 2016, has questioned whether success at university level translates into professional opportunities.

“Your success should also be your selector, but sometimes, unfortunately, that doesn’t happen,” Mokuena told IOL in 2020, identifying provincial unions as particularly important gatekeepers.

In South Africa, the question of who gets those opportunities is inseparable from race.

In 2022, 101 candidates were nominated by provincial unions for SA Rugby’s bespoke Elite Coaching Programme aimed at developing black coaches. Of the 18 selected, only 11, including Mokuena, completed the intensive 18-month programme.

title: Botham back as Morgan-Williams to make first start
article_text:
Wales flanker James Botham has been recalled by head coach Steve Tandy as one of five changes for the Nations Championship finale against Japan at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.

In the only backline alteration for the game in Twickenham, Ospreys scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams will make his first Wales start, with Tomos Williams named among the replacements.

Exeter lock Dafydd Jenkins will captain the side for the first time in more than two years with regular skipper Dewi Lake and flanker Jac Morgan also dropping to the bench.

Prop Rhys Carre and hooker Ryan Elias make their first starts of the November campaign, while lock Adam Beard returns at the expense of Ben Carter.

Wales have named an experienced bench that includes 294 caps.

Botham produced a player-of-the-match display in the 35-28 victory against New Zealand after making 30 tackles but was left out of the 29-26 defeat by Australia in favour of Cardiff colleague Alex Mann.

It was a decision which Botham’s father Liam, himself a former Cardiff wing, said Tandy had got wrong.

“I know there's a lot been spoken about it,” said Tandy.

“Everyone has got their opinions and people generally tell you who should be in the team and they never tell you who shouldn't.

“We're a tight group and as a coach I make sure I speak to all the players before if they are not selected. There'll be reasons why, whether it be bigger picture or whether it is form.

“I'll always speak to those, that's a special thing and the connection we feel in our environment.”

Botham, who became a father earlier this week, will play at open-side flanker against Japan after starring at blind-side against the All Blacks, with Mann and number eight Aaron Wainwright completing the back row.

“James was outstanding against the All Blacks, but we've got a back row depth there that we can move things around and freshen things up," said Tandy.

“James has had his little one, he's coming back in full of energy. We were so pleased for him things have gone well there."

Ospreys number nine Morgan-Williams is preparing for his first start in a position that has been dominated by Saracens scrum-half Williams during the Tandy era.

Williams has started 14 out of the 15 internationals, including the previous 11, with opportunities in short supply for others. But Williams came off early in the second half against Australia with a groin problem.

Carre, named Welsh rugby writers player of the 2025-26 season, is given his first start this autumn, with Nicky Smith dropping out of the squad.

Saracens loose-head Carre missed the first month of the season because of a hamstring injury and his only appearance of the autumn Tests so far was off the bench against Japan.

Elias, a replacement in the three previous November internationals, is handed his first Test start since the 2024 Six Nations match against France.

Montpellier lock Beard returns after missing the loss to Australia after suffering a shoulder injury against New Zealand.

Scarlets wing Ellis Mee is given his first involvement in the campaign after being named as a replacement.

Tandy has settled on his backline with full-back Blair Murray, wing Louis Rees-Zammit, centres Eddie James and Max Llewellyn and fly-half Sam Costelow starting all four matches in the November campaign as well as prop Archie Griffin and Jenkins.

Uncapped quartet Che Hope, Macs Page, Rhys Barratt and Aneurin Owen are among the players who will not be given game time, alongside Liam Belcher, Tom Rogers and Seb Davies, while Keiron Assiratti and Jarrod Evans have been late call-ups.

Wales have won three and lost three of their six Nations Championship matches to finish fifth in the northern hemisphere group, a position matched by Japan in the southern hemisphere section.

Wales will face Eddie Jones’ Japan side for a fifth time inside two years with Wales winning three out of the four games.

It is the first match of a Saturday double-header, with England and New Zealand to follow.

“We were frustrated and disappointed with losing last weekend,” said Tandy.

“We probably weren't as accurate as we could have been but there were a lot of positives in the performance to take also.

“We want to go out there, be ruthless and show improvement on our previous performance against Japan."

Jones has picked Auckland-born Tiennan Costley, normally a flanker, on the wing in a side again led by co-captains Warner Dearns and Naoto Saito.

Wales: Murray; Rees-Zammit, E James, Llewellyn, Adams: Costelow, Morgan-Williams; Carre, Elias, Griffin, D Jenkins (capt), Beard, Mann, Botham, Wainwright.

Replacements: Lake, G Thomas, Lewis, Plumtree, J Morgan, T Williams, Hawkins, Mee.

title: Marco van Staden disciplinary verdict: Five days on from Springboks red card
article_text:
Springboks supporters are still waiting to discover the outcome of Marco van Staden's disciplinary proceedings following his red card against Ireland.

The South African forward was sent off during Saturday's defeat in Dublin, leaving his availability for Sunday's Nations Championship final against France in doubt.

The wait comes at a particularly frustrating time for South Africa, with Pieter-Steph du Toit already ruled out of the final through injury.

Damian Willemse has also been forced to withdraw, leaving the Springboks facing a selection headache ahead of their showdown with France at Allianz Stadium.

Any suspension for Van Staden would further limit South Africa's back-row options.

With the inaugural Nations Championship final just days away, a decision is expected before the weekend.

However, no official timeframe for the announcement has been confirmed.

The disciplinary panel will determine whether the red card should be upheld and whether any further punishment is necessary, in accordance with World Rugby's disciplinary regulations.

RUCK will update this article with the full disciplinary verdict as soon as it is officially announced.

- Nickname: ‘Eskom’, because of his powerful tackling.

- Did you know? Van Staden played scrum-half for much of his schoolboy career before switching to the back row.

- Versatility: He has also played at hooker for the Springboks.

title: Cheslin Kolbe arrives in England ahead of Nations Championship final
article_text:
Cheslin Kolbe has arrived in London ahead of Sunday's Nations Championship final between the Springboks and France. Nothing suspicious about that, surely?

The double World Cup winner has been enjoying the sights of the English capital, sharing pictures from outside Buckingham Palace on Instagram with the caption: “Debut in London for her 🇬🇧”.

A bit of sightseeing, a curry and a romantic getaway. Lovely stuff.

Meanwhile, Damian Willemse and Pieter-Steph du Toit have been ruled out of Sunday's final, with SA Rugby confirming that Erasmus is still considering whether to call up a replacement.

Under any other international coach, this would be a completely innocent city break. Unfortunately for France, Rassie Erasmus has spent years making rugby fans question absolutely everything.

This is the man who turned a seven-one bench split into a genuine tactical weapon and had an entire rugby nation discussing the meaning of coloured traffic lights.

Would anyone really be surprised if Kolbe's sightseeing trip suddenly took an unexpected turn?

Home and Away Rugby even commented on his Instagram post: “See you on Sunday brother 🤝🇿🇦”.

Almost certainly a reference to attending the final as a spectator, but let's not allow common sense to spoil a perfectly good conspiracy theory.

Someone check whether he packed his boots.

There is, of course, no confirmation that Kolbe will join the Springboks squad.

The most likely explanation is that he is enjoying a well-earned break before cheering on his teammates from the stands at Allianz Stadium.

Although, judging by his holiday snaps, there's some serious carbohydrate loading going on. That portion of rice wasn't small.

Imagine trying to explain to your other half that a romantic weekend in London has suddenly turned into 80 minutes against France.

Perhaps Fabien Galthié should keep half an eye on the team sheet.

With any other international coach, I'd dismiss the idea entirely.

title: Six players to watch at the 2026 HSBC SVNS 3 in Dubai
article_text:
To say there the cream of the crop of sevens rugby will be taking the field in Dubai this weekend will be an understatement, with even the HSBC SVNS 3 competition stuffed to the brim with game-busting talent.

The respective qualifiers from regional tournaments in Africa, South America, North America Asia, Oceania and Europe, the 12 teams and 11 nations will feature some serious talent, with several having already played at Rugby World Cups, won major awards and more.

RugbyPass highlights six key players fans should keep an eye out for in the SVNS 3 competition, and who could potentially contribute to their sides qualifying for SVNS 2.

Starting with the Lady Cranes, Peace Lekuru played a major part in Uganda’s defeat of Kenya’s Lionesses 19-14 to qualify for this event in the Africa Rugby Sevens, scoring two key tries.

However, what was even more impressive was how well the Ugandan delivered under pressure, her second try coming in the final play of the game – and should her side push deep into the women’s tournament again, she will likely be called upon to deliver.

In a similar capacity, Zimbabwe find themselves in a similar place, surprising several teams in their Africa Rugby Sevens tournament to qualify for the men’s SVNS 3 – their victory seeing them defeat Uganda 26-19 in Kampala.

Ablant Tavonga had a big tournament for the Cheetahs, but his finest moment came with a try in the dying stages. His side will be hoping he can pull something similar out of the fire, with Zimbabwe facing tough competition in Hong Kong China, Samoa and Canada.

China might have come last in the inaugural season of SVNS 2 earlier this year, but all signs point to a side that is on the rise, having pushed Japan’s Sakura 7s team all the way in the Asia Rugby Sevens and at the 2026 Asian Games in Japan.

Yue Sun had a big campaign in both Japan and Sri Lanka, scoring all of her side’s points as they went down 14-7 to Japan in the final in Colombo – but with the result seeing them earn SVNS 3 qualification, the playmaker will look to show what she can really deliver in Dubai.

One of Hong Kong China’s most important dual internationals, Harry Sayers has been kept busy over the last few months, featuring heavily in his side’s World Nations Cup XVs campaign and their gold medal victories at the Asian Games and Asia Rugby Sevens series.

With him set to head to Australia in 2027 for the Rugby World Cup, a big victory for him and his side will come if they can qualify for SVNS 2, finishing in third last year and just missing out.

Samoa is set to be a significant wildcard in both their men’s and women’s sides this weekend, the only country to feature both their teams in SVNS 3 – however, with their women’s team fresh off the 2025 Rugby World Cup, expect them to bring a lot more experience to the forefront.

Their co-captain Saelua Leaula is one such player and is set for a critical campaign, delivering experience in a side that includes three debutants – but a time that oozes talent and potential if they can hit the ground running.

Lastly, the only side defending a SVNS 3 title, Canada’s men’s side will be looking for a better campaign this year after failing to qualify for the SVNS World Championship, finishing last in SVNS 2.

The Maple Leafs will bring in several players with Test rugby experience – several of whom are fresh off the Nations Cup – but the biggest to watch is two-time Major League Rugby title winner Brock Webster, who is the incumbent Major League Rugby Player of the Year after starring for the Chicago Hounds in the grand final.

title: 'I've spoken to all the players': Dave Rennie on the impending All Blacks exodus
article_text:
Rugby World Cups are both a celebration of the international rugby arena and the end of the road for some of its most dedicated warriors. On the latter point, dominoes are starting to fall for New Zealand.

Luke Jacobson has signed with Aviron Bayonnais in the first overseas deal to be announced, and Beauden Barrett is reportedly also Europe-bound with a Bristol Bears deal in place. Plenty more established All Blacks stars are off-contract after 2027, including captain Ardie Savea, who has described the coming Super Rugby season as his ‘last dance’, while Richie Mo’unga and Shannon Frizell only returned to New Zealand from Japan on short-term deals to compete for inclusion at the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

Several younger players’ contracts will also expire next year, including Wallace Sititi, who has been linked with Stade Français, while Fehi Fineanganofo will join Newcastle Red Bulls. All players who leave New Zealand forgo their All Blacks eligibility under New Zealand Rugby’s current laws.

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie himself is not contracted beyond the coming Rugby World Cup, but says he is across the current contract negotiations and that it would be hypocritical of him to warn his players against leaving New Zealand.

“I’m not surprised because I know about it. I’ve spoken to all the players who are maybe being mentioned,” Rennie told reporters in London.

“I think Luke’s official; any other stuff is unconfirmed, so I probably can’t talk about it yet. But I understand it. When you talk about Luke and other guys who played for 10-plus years in New Zealand, they’ve got an opportunity to make serious money, and it’s also getting exposed to a different culture and different lifestyle and that sort of thing, which is pretty exciting for family.

“So, I understand that you obviously want to keep players at home, but I mean I did the same as a coach. So it would be hypocritical of me to say you shouldn’t go.

“But ultimately, when we’ve got young players who are looking to go, you want to keep them, because you think they can play a hell of a long time in an All Black jersey. But some of those guys will sign for a couple of years, and a couple of years ends up being probably 17 months because they go at the end of an All Black season, and there’s about seven months left of the competition against whether it’s France or Japan or whatever, and then another year. So maybe 19 months they are away prior to coming back.”

Leicester Fainga’anuku is another whose contract runs only until next year, just two seasons after returning from a two-year stint in the Top 14 with Toulon. His decision, like Mo’unga’s and Frizell’s, could become the blueprint for young players within Rugby World Cup cycles.

Rennie isn’t opposed to players developing overseas and returning, given the benefits it’s delivered to the likes of Jordie Barrett and Rieko Ioane during their one-year sabbaticals at Leinster.

“I think it definitely depends on where you go to,” he explained. “I would say the same with guys going to Japan. If the guys can make massive money, then maybe it doesn’t matter where you go. But if your plan is to go away and come back better, then you choose wisely.

“So obviously Leinster’s a high-quality club, always in the race for titles. Yeah, and then I think obviously those guys get into play with a lot of the Irish internationals who are very smart; they’ve got good game sense and game awareness, and so they would have learned heaps.

“Good people involved from a staffing point of view. So there is no doubt that going to a quality club, you come back with an appreciation that the game is played a little bit differently. And so you look at Leinster, very, very structured. There’s no doubt that guys are coming back better.

“And even with a sabbatical, these guys are going away for a year; if they go to really good clubs, potentially they come back, outside of the fact maybe a bit richer, but a bit better, because they’ve been exposed to something different.”

title: ‘Throw the shackles off’: What Les Kiss wants from Wallabies against Ireland
article_text:
It’s been an up-and-down year for the Wallabies, who have claimed some historic wins and fallen to some comprehensive defeats. But as the Aussies now look to their final Test before a Rugby World Cup year, coach Les Kiss wants to see them “throw the shackles off” in attack.

Kiss succeeded Joe Schmidt as the new Wallabies head coach earlier this year, speaking often since then about the ‘Wallaby way’ and the team’s intent on doing the sports-mad nation proud. And in that time, the Wallabies have achieved some special feats.

The Wallabies claimed an unprecedented series victory away to Los Pumas earlier this year, winning the first Test and drawing the second. That match was followed by a memorable win over the Springboks in Perth, before a string of heavy defeats to fierce rivals.

New Zealand (twice) and England both put at least 43 points on the Aussies, who also fell in a closely fought battle with Scotland. But after bouncing back with a hard-earned result against an improving Welsh outfit, the Wallabies have their sights set on a season finale in London.

The Wallabies are preparing to face an Irish side who just beat the Springboks, battling for fifth place in the Nations Championship Finals Weekend. Kiss has identified some areas the Aussies must get right, hoping they can finish the 2026 off on a positive note.

“I hope the performance is one that the boys can really stretch their confidence and belief in the type of game they’re really working to,” Kiss said.

“We need to get the set-piece right, we need to get our defence right. We definitely need to do that. But in attack, hopefully they can throw the shackles off a bit and find a few things stick a bit more for them.

“I’d just like them to finish in a really strong way.

“It’s going to be tough against Ireland for sure. They’re a quality team and what they did to South Africa was tough last week. But go out there and give their all, be a team that makes Australia proud and let’s see what happens. It’ll be a good game.”

Kiss has sprung some selection shocks ahead of the season finale, with regular skipper Harry Wilson and 2026 John Eales Medallist Fraser McReight both shifting to the bench. 95-Test Wallaby Kurtley Beale is also in line to play his first Test in five years.

Former Northampton Saints winger James Ramm and NSW Waratahs scrum-half Teddy Wilson are both set to make their Test debuts. Kalani Thomas also comes into the starting side, with Ryan Lonergan and Tate McDermott both making way.

But the biggest talking point from Wednesday’s team announcement was the selection of Allan Alaalatoa as co-captain, in what will be the tighthead prop’s 100th cap. Alaalatoa joins Isaac Kailea and Brandon Paenga-Amosa in the front row.

“He carries the legacy of the jersey in such a beautiful way. He’s a wonderful character. His leadership style is unbelievable,” Kiss explained.

“The way he can hold a person to account and challenge them is really special. He can do it in a good way, in a tough way, but still be kind at the same time. People listen to him.

“He’s an impressive character. He’s someone that everyone looks up to.”

title: SALT, sisterhood and LA28: Fiji women’s rugby sevens is back on the rise
"Question of balance" - Steve Borthwick explains decision to leave Henry Pollock out
article_text:
Steve Borthwick has explained his decision to leave Henry Pollock on the bench for England's clash with the All Blacks on Saturday.

The Northampton Saints sensation has been one of England's standout performers this autumn, but Exeter Chiefs forward Greg Fisilau has been preferred in the starting XV.

The decision has divided supporters, with many questioning what more Pollock needs to do to earn a starting spot.

However, Borthwick insists the youngster is not the only player pushing for promotion from the bench.

“I enjoy what Henry has done off the bench,” said Borthwick.

“Another one, George Martin, a number of us could say, ‘George Martin has had so much impact, he could start’. It’s not just Henry, there’s a number of people.

“Marcus – every time Marcus comes on, how well does he play? Every time. These guys are doing such a good job at the end of games. They do such a good job in that latter third of the game.”

Remarkably, all eight of Pollock's England tries have come from the bench.

The 21-year-old's effectiveness against tiring opposition appears to be a major factor behind Borthwick's decision.

Borthwick also explained that Fisilau's ability at the breakdown influenced his selection against the All Blacks, who will be without injured superstar Will Jordan.

“There is always the question of balance. The balance of how many changes, the balance of what changes,” Borthwick continued.

“I talked about the breakdown, which is significant, and suits Greg’s skill set. I also like Henry coming on and playing against tired defenders with a bit more space.”

Ironically, Pollock's sensational performances from the bench may be working against his chances of becoming a regular starter.

With England recording a commanding 37-12 victory over New Zealand last weekend, Borthwick clearly sees little reason to abandon a winning formula.

For now, one of English rugby's brightest young talents remains its most dangerous replacement.

title: Two nations remain banned from Rugby World Cups after failed appeal
article_text:
Russia and Belarus remain banned from international rugby, with a bid to overturn Russia's suspension proving unsuccessful.

Both nations have been excluded from international competition since February 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

World Rugby imposed an indefinite suspension on both countries, preventing their national teams from participating in international rugby and cross-border competitions.

Russia's attempts to overturn the suspension have so far failed to secure a return to international rugby.

Neither nation will feature at the expanded 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia, which will see 24 teams compete for the Webb Ellis Cup for the first time.

Russia previously appeared at the 2011 and 2019 Rugby World Cups, facing the likes of Ireland, Australia, Scotland and Japan across those tournaments.

However, Russia has not featured at the tournament since its appearance in Japan.

Belarus, meanwhile, has never qualified for a Rugby World Cup.

Before its suspension, Russia had ambitions to become a more prominent force in international rugby.

The country had even expressed an interest in hosting the 2031 Rugby World Cup, which was subsequently awarded to the United States.

Russia also hosted the Rugby World Cup Sevens in Moscow in 2013.

Those ambitions have since been put on hold.

World Rugby's original suspension was imposed indefinitely rather than for a fixed period.

That means there is no automatic return date for either nation.

With the 2027 tournament now out of reach, the 2031 Rugby World Cup in the United States represents the next potential opportunity.

However, both countries would need to have their suspensions lifted and successfully navigate the qualification process.

For now, their international rugby exile continues.

title: Alaalatoa hits 100 for Wallabies as fellow veteran ends 4-year Test exile
article_text:
Veteran prop Allan Alaalatoa will become the 14th Wallabies centurion when he runs out onto Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, against Ireland on Friday night.

Ten years have passed since Alaalatoa made his debut against New Zealand in a 42-8 defeat at the ANZ Stadium in Sydney.

He will co-captain the side with Harry Wilson, who drops to the bench, for the Wallabies’ final Test of 2026.

After patiently waiting for his first cap, Sydney-born James Ramm has been brought into the team on the wing.

A one-time Olympics gymnast hopeful, Ramm makes his debut in the country where he rediscovered his love for the game during a spell at title-winning Northampton Saints.

Now with Western Force, the 28-year-old is joined in the matchday 23 by another uncapped player in reserve scrum-half, Teddy Wilson.

The former Junior Wallabies captain in line to become the 16th son of a Wallaby to pull on the gold jersey, following in the footsteps of his father David who featured in two Rugby World Cups, including the 1999 side that lifted the Webb Ellis Cup in Cardiff.

A quarter of a century ago, his father played his club rugby across the road from the Allianz Stadium at the Twickenham Stoop after signing for the world-famous Harlequins.

Elsewhere, Kurtley Beale has earned a remarkable recall to the gold jersey – named on the bench, four years since his last Test appearance. Beale is four caps behind Alaalatoa and has made more appearances for the Wallabies than the starting back-three combined.

Kalani Thomas has earned his first Test start at scrum-half alongside club teammate, Carter Gordon.

Wallabies Head Coach Les Kiss said: “Reaching 100 Test matches for your country is a remarkable achievement and it’s only fitting that Allan leads the side out as co-captain for such a monumental occasion.

“He is a talismanic figure within the group, and I know the whole squad and support staff will be doing everything they can to make this rare milestone a memorable one for him, his family and for us.

“We’ve taken some steps forward, grown our game and tested our squad depth this year as a squad and I know the team is highly motivated to put in a performance that reflects the hard work put in by everyone in our final Test.”

title: South America Rugby World Cup 2035 Bid Takes Step Forward
article_text:
As part of the formal bidding process, a multinational working group had already completed a detailed questionnaire covering every proposed venue and host nation. The subsequent online meeting allowed the South American delegation to formally present its vision to twelve Rugby World Cup representatives joining from London and Dublin, followed by a Q&A session addressing specific inquiries.

(A). The Power of Amateur Club Culture: Officials emphasized the central social, familial, emotional, and sporting role of local clubs across the region, positioning grassroots rugby as a foundational pillar of the tournament.

(B). World-Class Tourism: Supported by a promotional video, the delegation highlighted the diverse destinations awaiting visiting fans across the four nations and wider continent—from Patagonia and Iguazu Falls (bordering three countries) to the Atacama Desert and the beaches of Punta del Este and Rio de Janeiro.

(C). Proven Event-Hosting Capacity: The bid underscored South America’s track record of successfully staging massive global gatherings, citing the Olympic Games, the Youth Olympic Games, the FIFA World Cup, major international concerts, MotoGP, Formula One, and Pope Leo XIV’s recent visit to Uruguay and Argentina, which drew millions of attendees with seamless organization.

Former Puma Horacio Agulla, a three-time World Cup veteran (2007, 2011, and 2015) and active member of the bid team, noted that the presentation was warmly received.

“Since it was a Zoom call, we could have done it from an office, but we wanted the importance and symbolism of the clubs as the center of our bid to be crystal clear. It is a differentiator that we are looking to leverage”

“We are convinced that a World Cup in our region will have full stadiums, all the appeal of tourism, and—as an X-factor—the passion and love we feel for rugby, which is born in the clubs.”

The next phase of the candidacy will be an on-site technical visit by Rugby World Cup officials to inspect each proposed venue across the region. Following that tour, additional questionnaires and evaluations will take place in early 2027 to finalize assurances before the World Rugby Executive Board selects and announces the 2035 host in November 2027.
