title: Sinner Issues Update on Knee Surgery
article_text:
Jannik Sinner underwent successful right knee surgery in Finland today—and will require at least three months to recover, Italian media reports.

The 25-year-old Sinner had successful right knee surgery in Turku, Finland today, Dr. Herbert Schönhuber, a sports physician, told Italy’s RaiNews.

Sinner confirmed the surgery with this social media post today.

“After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn’t respond as we’d all hoped, that’s why today I understand a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band,” Sinner said in a post on X. “I really miss being on court and will now begin my recovery process together with my team.

Over the past few months, together with my team we’ve tried everything to treat my injury without surgery. After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn’t respond as we’d all hoped, that’s why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band. I really miss being on court and will now begin my recovery process together with my team. Thank you for all your support. See you soon! ❤️ Jannik

Italian journalist Gabriele Parpiglia reported Sinner is suffering from Iliotibial Band Syndrome above his right knee, a condition common in distance runners, Johns Hopkins reports.

Two-time Wimbledon winner Sinner had surgery performed by orthopedic surgeon Dr. Lasse Lempainen, who had examined the Italian superstar last weekend in Milan, according to Italian media.

“As part of the operation, the Finnish specialist lengthened the so-called iliotibial ligament – a strong tendon strip that runs along the outside of the thigh up to the knee,” RaiNews reported today. “According to Herbert Schönhuber, this very method was the most medically gentle and stress-relieving solution to permanently resolve the tennis professional’s persistent complaints.”

Sinner’s expected recovery time is about three months, which means he will almost certainly miss the 2027 Australian Open, which begins in January.

Sinner won the 2024 and 2025 Australian Open titles before bowing to Novak Djokovic at the Melbourne major in January. Carlos Alcaraz defeated Djokovic in the AO final becoming the youngest man in history to complete the career Grand Slam.

Five-time Grand Slam champion Sinner has not played a match since successfully defending his Wimbledon championship with a 6-7(7), 7-6(2), 6-3, 6-4 triumph over Alexander Zverev on Centre Court on July 12th.

Down a set, Sinner snuffed out the second seed’s threat holding in all 22 service games, saving the lone break point he faced and firing 15 aces against only 2 double faults.

Sinner posted a 44-3 record with six tournaments titles in 2026.

Currently ranked No. 2, Sinner is 350 rankings points ahead of ATP Finals champion and world No. 3 Carlos Alcaraz. If Sinner does indeed miss the 2027 Australian Open, he will lose 800 ranking points from the Melbourne major.

title: Renowned News Outlet Strikes $11 Million ATP Deal To Promote Tennis Across Its Home Nation
article_text:
French tennis enthusiasts are set to be treated to a familiar name on their television screens. beIN Sports has won back the rights to the ATP Tour in France from 2028, and it hasn’t cost them an arm and a leg. According to L’Equipe, the Franco-Qatari channel will pay a little under 10 million euros, roughly 11 million dollars, a year across a four-year deal running to 2031, a deliberately restrained outlay for such a prized property.

The move, confirmed on 9 November, amounts to a homecoming of sorts. beIN Sports will broadcast the ATP in France before Eurosport got the rights, which means that the rights to the men’s tour are back on the channel. This time, however, it is coming back on its own terms – at a price that is more indicative of a leaner, more disciplined era in the business of broadcast rights than any of the crazy bidding that has occurred in the past few years.

The sum says a good deal about beIN’s current thinking. It sits only marginally above the roughly 5 million euros a year that the outgoing rights holder, Eurosport, has been paying, and it barely registers against the budgets the channel has shed elsewhere. A few years ago, beIN walked away from a contract in Ligue 1 that was worth about 85.6 million dollars a year and has recently lost a contract in La Liga that was worth some 34.9 million dollars, giving it much more freedom to pick and choose its fights.

But it’s a mantra that’s become familiar to Yousef al-Obaidly, head of beIN Sports France, who has always said that one should spend smartly, not buy rights for the sake of buying rights. Securing the men’s tour for a modest fee, having stepped back from costlier football deals, fits neatly into that philosophy. For beIN, it is a way of strengthening its sporting line-up without the financial exposure that top-tier football now demands, a trade-off the channel appears increasingly comfortable making.

All nine ATP Masters 1000 events will be broadcast on beIN from 2028, and all ATP 500 and the Next Gen ATP Finals will also be broadcast on beIN, which is also being reported as having the ATP Finals as part of the deal at the end of the season. It’s a complete men’s offering, a package that will transform the sport’s presence at the start of the decade in France and round off a tennis collection that the broadcaster has been steadily assembling over the past few years.

beIN Sports is no newcomer to the game. The broadcaster already has the rights to the WTA Tour and to Wimbledon, so this adds the men’s circuit to the mix for a nearly full calendar. It will be a great selling point for subscribers as the majority of the top events of the season will come together under one roof starting in 2028, minus a few exceptions, when sports coverage is spread out across increasingly more platforms.

For Eurosport, the deal brings a long association with the ATP towards its end. Next year, the Warner Bros. Discovery-owned channel will air one final season of the men’s tour, but not everything is moving over at the same time.

Two French ATP 250 tournaments have been confirmed for Tennis Channel, and Eurosport has secured the future of the Australian Open and the US Open beyond 2030, ensuring it will have a role to play in the sport even after it stops hosting ATP events.

The upshot is that French coverage will be split across more than one home from 2028, with two of the four Grand Slams staying where they are while the week-to-week tour action moves on, a division viewers will have to get used to.

The reshuffle reflects a wider trend in the sports-rights market, where broadcasters have become more hesitant to pay top dollar, and sellers are forced to agree to lower figures than the glory days dictated.

While the headline fee isn’t jaw-dropping, but the committed signing until 2031 is a solid piece of stability for the ATP. The bottom line for French TV viewers is even more straightforward, as the way to watch the men’s game will go through beIN Sports from 2028.

There will surely be subscription fee and reach questions, as beIN is behind a paywall, but at least it ends the uncertainty that hung over the tour’s French future.

title: Thailand’s ‘View’ Kunlavut reclaims world No 1 badminton ranking
article_text:
Thailand’s badminton star Kunlavut “View” Vitidsarn has reclaimed the world No 1 spot in the men’s singles rankings following the latest update announced by the Badminton World Federation (BWF) on Tuesday (November 24).

The 25-year-old Thai shuttler moved up from second place with 91,585 ranking points, overtaking France’s Christo Popov, who dropped to second with 89,932 points.

Kunlavut’s return to the summit follows a series of impressive performances throughout 2026, highlighted by his historic Asian Games gold medal and runner-up finish at the Hong Kong Open.

Kunlavut reached the final of the Hong Kong Open 2026 but was forced to withdraw from the championship match against Denmark’s Anders Antonsen on Sunday (November 22) because of a back injury.

Antonsen was consequently awarded the title by walkover, while Kunlavut finished runner-up at the BWF World Tour Super 500 tournament.

Despite the injury setback, the Thai star earned enough ranking points to regain the world No 1 position, marking his fourth spell at the top of the men’s singles rankings.

Kunlavut first became world No 1 on June 3, 2025, following his Singapore Open triumph, becoming the first Thai men’s singles badminton player to reach the top of the world rankings.

He returned to No 1 in March 2026 following his run to the All England Open semi-finals before reclaiming the position again after winning gold at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.

On September 29, Kunlavut defeated Singapore’s Loh Kean Yew 21-12, 21-16 to secure Thailand’s first-ever Asian Games gold medal in men’s singles badminton.

His latest rise to the top caps another remarkable chapter in his career and underlines his standing among the world’s elite badminton players.

title: Malaysia's World Tour Finals contingent shrinks to just two pairs
article_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia will have just two pairs at next month's World Tour Finals in Hangzhou, China, marking the country's smallest representation since 2023 despite another productive season on the international badminton circuit.

Men's doubles Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin Rumsani and women's doubles Pearly Tan-M. Thinaah are the only Malaysians to have secured qualifying spots for the Dec 9-13 showpiece, following the conclusion of the Hong Kong Open on Sunday.

After having six entries in 2024 and five last year, Malaysia's tally matches the joint-lowest representation since the BWF World Tour replaced the Super Series circuit in 2018, with just two pairs fielded in 2018, 2019 and 2023.

Although having more representatives does not necessarily guarantee success, the decline means fewer Malaysians will have the opportunity to compete against the season's best performers while reaping substantial financial and ranking rewards.

This year's World Tour Finals will offer a record US$3.5mil (RM14.41 million) in total prize money, an increase of US$500,000 (RM2.06 million) from last year, making it the richest tournament in badminton history.

The doubles champions stand to pocket a staggering US$294,000 (RM1.21 million) per pair, almost three times the US$107,3000 (RM442,000) awarded to the winners of this year's prestigious All England, a Super 1000 tournament.

Even finishing fourth and last in the group stage is worth approximately US$24,500 (RM100,900) for a doubles pair, considerably more than the US$19,000 (RM78,200) earned by the runners-up at last Sunday's Hong Kong Open.

The ranking benefits are equally attractive, with a fourth-place group finish earning 7,800 points, equivalent to reaching the final of a Super 500 tournament and slightly more than making the semi-finals of a Super 750 event.

For those who advance further, the financial rewards increase significantly, with the doubles runners-up earning approximately US$140,000 (RM576,500) and losing semi-finalists US$70,000 (RM288,300) per pair.

While Malaysia's representation may be limited this year, both qualifying pairs have strong credentials to challenge for honours.

World No. 5 Sze Fei-Izzuddin will be making their second appearance, having finished runners-up on their debut in 2024.

The independent pair came agonisingly close to becoming Malaysia's first World Tour Finals champions that year before losing to Denmark's Kim Astrup-Anders Skaarup Rasmussen in the final.

They failed to qualify last year but have bounced back strongly this season, winning the Indonesia Masters in January and the prestigious Indonesia Open in June.

Their consistency was further underlined by runners-up finishes at the Malaysia Masters and French Open, helping them secure a return to Hangzhou.

Pearly-Thinaah, meanwhile, will be making their fifth appearance at the season-ending tournament, although their breakthrough only came last year when they reached the semi-finals for the first time.

The world No. 4 previously failed to progress beyond the group stage in 2021, 2022 and 2024, while missing qualification in 2023.

Their campaign last year ended with a semi-final defeat to Japan's Yuki Fukushima-Mayu Matsumoto.

However, Pearly-Thinaah will head into this year's edition in encouraging form after capturing three titles, including Sunday's Hong Kong Open triumph.

They also won the Indonesia Masters and Denmark Open, besides finishing runners-up at the French Open and Taiwan Open.

Malaysia have yet to produce a World Tour Finals champion since the competition entered the World Tour era in 2018.

The country's closest attempts came in 2024, when Sze Fei-Izzuddin and mixed doubles pair Chen Tang Jie-Toh Ee Wei both reached the finals but settled for runners-up finishes.

Last year, Pearly-Thinaah and Tang Jie-Ee Wei made the semi-finals but were unable to progress further.

title: Aaron Tai-Roy King eye top 10 after stunning World Tour start
article_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: New men's doubles sensation Aaron Tai-Yap Roy King, buoyed by their impressive World Tour start, is looking to break into the top 10, aided by a favourable 15-point scoring system set to be introduced next year.

Aaron Tai-Roy King, who began their partnership at the European swing last month, won their first tournaments as a pair at the Arctic Open before adding the Kumamoto Masters title two weeks ago. Both were Super 500 events.

The Malacca-born duo have made a meteoric rise in the world rankings and are now ranked world No. 34 after playing in just six World Tour events.

After finishing their season at the Hong Kong Open last week, where they reached the last 16, Aaron Tai-Roy King will hope to continue their climb in the rankings and chase more honours under the 15-point scoring system, which favours their fast, aggressive style of play.

"We hope to push for the top 10 next year. We have a little advantage but in the 15-point scoring, anything can happen, so we need to be more focused," said the soft-spoken Aaron Tai at the Academy Badminton Malaysia (ABM) on Tuesday.

Aaron Tai also expressed surprise at their progress and attributed their success on the World Tour to their fluid combination and speed.

"I am definitely surprised by the way we have progressed because we have just started as a pair," added Aaron Tai.

"This was possible because his gameplay and mine are almost similar. We are fast and can combine well (on court)."

However, the 20-year-old former world junior champion also wants to iron out some of his weaknesses, especially his unforced errors and tendency to become too desperate to attack.

"I need to improve my consistency and also reduce errors. I also need to be patient when executing my shots and not rush," said Aaron Tai.

National men's doubles head coach Herry Iman Pierngadi was impressed with their speedy progress and made them permanent members of the squad after they reached the semi-finals of their third tournament, the Super 500 Hylo Open in Saarbrucken, Germany, last month.

Herry also believes their aggressive nature will make them Malaysia's most dangerous pair and even rated the youngsters higher than their seniors — world No. 4 Aaron Chia-Soh Wooi Yik and world No. 7 Man Wei Chong-Tee Kai Wun.

Their current world No. 34 ranking should still earn them a place in the Malaysia Open, scheduled for Jan 21-31, despite the tournament's top 32 cut-off for men's doubles pairs.

This is because both players are also ranked inside the top 32 with other partners. Aaron Tai is ranked No. 23 with Kang Khai Xing, while Roy King is No. 28 with Wan Arif Junaidi.

However, these two combinations will not be entered for the Super 1000 event, allowing Aaron Tai-Roy King to secure a place in the tournament.

title: Indonesia Sends Three Entries to $3.5 Million BWF World Tour Finals
article_text:
Indonesia Sends Three Entries to $3.5 Million BWF World Tour Finals

Jakarta. Indonesia is set to field five badminton players across three categories at the prestigious BWF World Tour Finals in Hangzhou, China, from Dec. 9 to 13, following the conclusion of the Race to Finals qualification standings at the 2026 Hong Kong Open.

Indonesia's representatives are Alwi Farhan in men's singles, Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohibul Fikri in men's doubles, and Amallia Cahaya Pratiwi and Siti Fadia Silva Ramadhanti in women's doubles.

The five shuttlers will be looking to end Indonesia's three-edition absence from the tournament's championship matches. The country's last finalists were Anthony Sinisuka Ginting in men's singles and Mohammad Ahsan and Hendra Setiawan in men's doubles, who finished as runners-up in 2022.

Alwi has emerged as one of Indonesia's standout performers this season, securing a place at the World Tour Finals for the first time in his career.

The 21-year-old faces formidable competition in men's singles, with a field featuring 2026 world champion Alex Lanier, defending champion Christo Popov and other leading players, including Kunlavut Vitidsarn and Anders Antonsen.

The men's singles lineup is particularly notable for the absence of Chinese representatives among the eight qualifiers. Europe, meanwhile, accounts for three places through French players Lanier and Popov and Denmark's Antonsen.

Fajar and Fikri will be looking to improve on their performance at the 2025 World Tour Finals, where they were eliminated in the group stage.

The Indonesian pair will compete against some of the world's leading men's doubles partnerships, including South Korea's Kim Won-ho and Seo Seung-jae, China's Liang Wei Keng and Wang Chang, and Malaysia's Goh Sze Fei and Nur Izzuddin Rumsani.

In women's doubles, Amallia and Siti Fadia secured their qualification after reaching the semifinals of the Hong Kong Open.

The Indonesian duo will face a competitive field that includes China's Liu Sheng Shu and Tan Ning, South Korea's Baek Ha-na and Lee So-hee, and Malaysia's Pearly Tan and Thinaah Muralitharan.

The 2026 BWF World Tour Finals offers a total prize pool of $3.5 million, up from $3 million in the previous edition.

The season-ending tournament brings together eight players or pairs in each of five categories. Participants are divided into two groups of four, with the top two finishers in each group advancing to the semifinals.

The final lineup remains subject to the Badminton World Federation's formal invitation and acceptance process.

Invitations are scheduled to be issued on Nov. 24, with players required to confirm their participation by Nov. 27. The group-stage draw is scheduled for Dec. 5.

title: Syed Modi International 2026: Full schedule, Indians in action, prize money, and all you need to know
article_text:
Despite the absence of P. V. Sindhu and Lakshya Sen, India will have a formidable contingent taking part in the Syed Modi India International 2026 Super 300, which gets underway in Lucknow on November 24 and runs until November 29.

H.S. Prannoy, Tanvi Sharma, Unnati Hooda, Treesa-Gayatri, Arjun-Hariharan and Dhruv-Tanisha will all be in action at the Babu Banarasi Das U.P. Badminton Academy Stadium.

title: Three Indonesian Representatives Qualify for 2026 BWF World Tour Finals
2026 Davis Cup Finals prize money confirmed as Alcaraz, Zverev, and Cobolli battle for the title
article_text:
The ATP Tour season may be done, but some of the biggest names in men’s tennis still have one more event to compete at: the Davis Cup Finals in Bologna.

Taking place inside the Supertennis Arena, Davis Cup Finals action will start on Tuesday, with eight nations all hoping they will lift the title come Sunday’s showpiece.

Each tie will consist of two singles rubbers followed by a deciding doubles rubber, if the tie is level at 1-1 following the opening singles matches.

Hosts Italy enter as the three-time defending champions and are among the favourites to triumph once again, though could face stiff competition from the likes of Spain, Germany, and Czechia.

One of the most famous titles in tennis is up for grabs, but there will also be significant prize money on offer in Bologna.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

What prize money is on offer in Bologna?

As per the Davis Cup website, there is a total prize money pool of $4,900,000 on offer in Bologna this year, to be split across the eight competing nations.

All eight countries have guaranteed a minimum payout of $350,000, which will be the total prize money paycheck for the four nations that exit the Finals at the quarter-final stage.

The two beaten semi-finalist nations will take home $500,000, while the runner-up nation in Sunday’s final will earn $1,000,000 for reaching the final.

The victorious nation will earn an impressive $1,500,000 for lifting the title in Bologna.

It is up to each individual nation as to how they wish to split prize money between each member of their squad.

The biggest name in action is world No 3 and seven-time Grand Slam champion Carlos Alcaraz, who confirmed after his ATP Finals triumph on Sunday that he still intended to represent his country in Bologna this week.

Alcaraz has never lifted the Davis Cup title, and will hope his team — which includes world No 10 Rafael Jodar — can triumph for Spain’s first triumph since 2019, and end David Ferrer’s spell as captain on a high.

Spain take on Austria in their quarter-final on Thursday, and the winner of that tie will face the winner of the quarter-final between Germany and Great Britain.

Germany’s squad is still set to be headlined by world No 1 Alexander Zverev, who will hope he can guide his nation to a first title in the men’s team competition since 1993.

Zverev is joined by the likes of Jan-Lennard Struff in the German team, while the Great Britain team is headlined by Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery.

The first quarter-final of the event takes place on Tuesday, with Czechia taking on Canada.

The Czech team is one of the strongest in the event, led by world No 14 Jiri Lehecka and world No 15 Jakub Mensik, while world No 17 Felix Auger-Aliassime is Canada’s star man.

Hosts Italy take to court on Wednesday for their quarter-finals versus South Korea, and have an incredibly strong team consisting of Flavio Cobolli, Luciano Darderi, Lorenzo Musetti, and Matteo Berrettini.

If Italy triumph, they would become the first nation to lift four consecutive Davis Cup titles since the United States won the event in five consecutive years from 1968-1972.

The highest-ranked player in the South Korea team is world No 139 Soon-Woo Kwon.

title: Henry Patten ends partnership with Harri Heliovaara to team up with fellow Briton Neal Skupski
article_text:
Henry Patten has ended his world No 1 doubles partnership with Harri Heliovaara in shock fashion in favour of teaming up with British compatriot Neal Skupski for 2027.

Patten and Heliovaara celebrated being crowned the best men's doubles team of the year at last week's ATP Finals after they claimed a second Wimbledon success together back in July.

However, in a post on Heliovaara's blog, the Finnish player revealed Patten phoned him on Friday to say their three-time Grand Slam-winning partnership was over - despite a previous agreement they would continue.

"After the trip to Turin, I didn't even have time to get into the holiday mood when the weekend took a rather unexpected turn," Heliovaara said on his own blog website. "Henry completely unexpectedly announced that he had changed his mind about next year.

"I picked up the kids from daycare on Friday afternoon and we were just opening presents when I got a call from Henry. Without going into too much detail, the message was clear.

"He didn't want to play together again next year, even though we had agreed to do so during the fall. The announcement came as completely as it could come and I couldn't help but listen with my mouth open in horror and say that I don't agree at all.

"I'm unlikely to ever fully understand what and why this ultimately happened.

"The emotional scale in my head was quite violent at first, a shocking situation in any case.

"The two-and-a-half years with Henry have been by far the best time of my career, for which I am eternally grateful to him, but now the main feeling was heavy disappointment and even anger."

Heliovaara confirmed in his blog that he would team up with another British player Julian Cash, while Patten is set to partner Skupski in 2027.

title: How Jannik Sinner’s injury could affect ATP Rankings with Carlos Alcaraz & Alexander Zverev set to benefit
article_text:
What appeared to be a minor niggle at first now looks to be a serious problem for Jannik Sinner, with the Italian’s injury absence now seemingly set to extend well into 2027.

World No 2 Sinner is reportedly set to undergo surgery in Finland on Tuesday to deal with his ongoing knee injury, with indications that he is dealing with iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS).

Sinner has not played since Wimbledon due to the issue, skipping the US Open and the ATP Finals, among other events, and he now looks likely to miss several more key events next season.

There are indications that Sinner could be out until April next year, a situation that would affect him greatly in the ATP Rankings — and give a big opportunity to Alexander Zverev and Carlos Alcaraz.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

All indications regarding Sinner’s surgery suggest that, at the very least, he will be unable to compete at the Australian Open in January 2027.

The Italian is a two-time champion in Melbourne and was a semi-finalist at the event in 2026, falling to Novak Djokovic in a thrilling five-set encounter.

Assuming that Sinner is unable to play at the Australian Open, he would drop the 800 ranking points he is defending at the event. That would see him fall from 7,950 points to 7,150 points.

That would all but guarantee he loses ground to world No 1 Zverev, who is also defending 800 points following his own semi-final run in Melbourne back in January.

Prior to the Australian Open, the German will drop 40 points from the United Cup, but could win up to 250 points at the Brisbane International instead.

Zverev is effectively guaranteed to remain as the world No 1 post-Australian Open, but could surge to over 11,500 points should he win the title in Melbourne — and potentially sit over 4,000 points ahead of Sinner.

However, assuming he is absent, Sinner could well find himself still ahead of Alcaraz in the ATP Rankings at that point.

Currently 350 points separate world No 2 Sinner and world No 3 Alcaraz, who holds 7,600 points in the ATP Rankings after his triumph at the ATP Finals on Sunday.

The Spaniard is the defending Australian Open champion and has a full 2,000 points to his name from the tournament, meaning his best hope rankings-wise is to defend the title and remain on 7,600 points.

If Sinner was absent, that would see Alcaraz move back to world No 2 post-Melbourne, but any other result for the Spaniard would keep the Italian ahead in the ATP Rankings.

With some suggestions that Sinner could be out for three to four months, all eyes will be on when he returns — and what points he might drop in the mean time.

The Italian will have just 100 points to defend at the Qatar Open in February, though will then have 1,000 points to defend in both Indian Wells and Miami, having completed the ‘Sunshine Double’ back in March of this year.

If Sinner was to also miss these events after also missing the Australian Open, he would lose a further 2,100 points and drop to 5,050 points in the ATP Rankings.

Hypothetically, that would see him drop further behind both Alcaraz and Zverev, and both men would have the chance to surge ahead of the Italian significantly.

Across that same stretch, Zverev has just 50 points to defend at the Acapulco Open, and then 400 points each at both Indian Wells and the Miami Open, a total of 850 points that is 1,250 points less than Sinner’s equivalent.

Meanwhile, Alcaraz will have 500 points to defend as the reigning Qatar Open champion in February, but then just 400 points in Indian Wells and a mere 50 points at the Miami Open.

Obviously, Sinner will have a notable chance to gain points across the second half of the season, having not played since Wimbledon this year. He also has just 50 points to defend at the French Open, following his shock exit in round two in May.

However, there is no denying that if his injury is as serious as feared, he could find himself trailing both Zverev and Alcaraz significantly when he returns.

title: Enyo leads Premier Golf League claim against PGA Tour
LIV Golf star confirms shock HotelPlanner Tour move amid uncertain future
article_text:
Former LIV Golf star Marc Leishman has secured membership on the HotelPlanner Tour for the 2027 season, providing the Australian with another route back to competition as he works out the next chapter of his playing career.

Leishman's name featured among the confirmed membership categories released by the HotelPlanner Tour on Thursday, following the deadline for players to take up their playing rights earlier this week.

The development offers some clarity over Leishman's immediate future after the 43-year-old admitted his playing plans remained uncertain following the collapse of LIV Golf, where he spent the previous four seasons competing alongside fellow Australian Cameron Smith at Ripper GC.

Leishman, a six-time winner on the PGA Tour, enjoyed considerable success during his time with the Saudi-bankrolled league, claiming his only LIV Golf individual victory at LIV Golf Miami in April 2025 with a one-shot triumph.

However, with his position on the professional golf landscape now changing, membership of the HotelPlanner Tour could provide an important opportunity to rebuild his status and work towards a return to the DP World Tour.

A total of 258 players representing 40 different countries have secured exemptions across Categories 1-16 for the 2027 Road to Mallorca season.

Among those are 21 players who earned their playing rights through the Official Satellite Tours, including the Nordic Golf League, Alps Tour, Pro Golf Tour, Clutch Pro Tour, Tartan Pro Tour and MENA Tour. Four of those players subsequently improved their category through performances on the DP World Tour or at Qualifying School.

A further 15 players progressed through the DP World Tour Final Stage of Qualifying School, finishing outside the top 15 and ties but inside the top 40 and ties to secure Category 9 status. Three additional players earned their places through their positions in the 2026 Global Amateur Pathway Ranking.

Leishman is also one of 36 former DP World Tour winners who have taken up membership for the upcoming campaign.

That group includes a number of established names, such as former winners Byeong Hun An, Eddie Pepperell, Ross Fisher, Marcel Siem, Matthieu Pavon, Pablo Larrazábal, George Coetzee, Kiradech Aphibarnrat, Dylan Frittelli and John Catlin.

Other notable players on the list include Chris Wood, Tom Lewis, Edoardo Molinari, Alexander Levy, Shubhankar Sharma, Daniel Gavins, Yannik Paul, Jesper Svensson, Rikuya Hoshino and Ryggs Johnston.

The full list of exempt members and their respective categories is available through the official HotelPlanner Tour website.

The 2027 Road to Mallorca gets underway on January 21 with the SDC Open, the first of four consecutive co-sanctioned tournaments with the Sunshine Tour. The complete tournament schedule is expected to be announced in December 2026.

For Leishman, however, membership represents just one part of a playing future that remains far from settled.

Speaking ahead of this week's Australian PGA Championship, which marks the beginning of the 2027 DP World Tour season, the six-time PGA Tour winner admitted he had no playing status anywhere for next year.

Notably, Leishman was not among the nine former LIV Golf players offered invitations onto the DP World Tour for the new season, leaving him to explore alternative opportunities.

He also made it clear that, despite retaining his ambition to compete at the highest level, he has little desire to return to the demanding full-time schedule that defined much of his career.

Therefore a potential route back onto the DP World Tour via the HotelPlanner Tour would seem an unlikely one for the talented Australian.

Having also spent lengthy periods away from his family in Virginia Beach, Leishman is now keen to strike a better balance during the latter stages of his playing career.

His immediate focus is therefore on a series of tournaments in Australia, having added the Players Series event at Peninsula Kingswood in January to his schedule alongside the Victorian PGA and Australian PGA Championship.

Strong performances could put him in contention for the PGA Tour of Australasia's Order of Merit, which also offers a pathway to DP World Tour membership.

Leishman has indicated he would consider adding further tournaments if he believed he had a realistic opportunity of winning the season-long standings.

"I'll do what I have to do," Leishman said ahead of the Australian PGA Championship at The Lakes GC in Sydney.

"I certainly don't want to go back to playing and being away for more than half the year from my family again. I feel like I am past that grind.

"I want to play the big events and I have an opportunity these next two weeks to play my way into big events. If I was to have a really good week this week that can get me some good status on the DP World Tour.

"As far as playing a full, full schedule again, I don't know if I am motivated to do that. I certainly want to keep competing above that part of golf, testing yourself under pressure.

"You never say never, I'll play where I have to play to get status back."

Away from competition, Leishman has also begun exploring opportunities in golf course design, taking a leading role in the redevelopment of the former Signature at West Neck course in Virginia Beach.

Working alongside fellow Australian and 1991 Open Championship winner Ian Baker-Finch, the project is set to become known as The Turn 757 and will feature a new nine-hole course, driving range and renovated clubhouse.

It is an avenue Leishman has been keen to explore as he prepares for life beyond professional golf, although he remains determined to extend his playing career for as long as possible.

title: Tiger Woods Suffers Legal Setback Ahead Of Latest Comeback
article_text:
As Tiger Woods prepares for his highly-anticipated return to tournament golf, his off course business dealings suffered a bit of a speed bump in a California court.

Woods' Sun Day Red brand built alongside TaylorMade has been embroiled in a long-running trademark dispute with Louisiana cooling company Tigeraire.

The battle stems from the company logos being similar in that they're both leaping tiger motifs, with the legal challenge being launched against it right after Sun Day Red launched in February 2024.

Woods is busy preparing for his latest comeback at the Hero World Challenge in the Bahamas, from 3-6 December, and will likely just be letting the lawyers deal with the case - but it's still an unwanted hurdle that could affect Sun Day Red's ability to grow in the future.

The 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 2-1 against Sun Day Red this week to overturn a previous decision on a lawsuit it filed to clarify it had not infringed on Tigeraire's trademark.

Tigeraire makes personal cooling fans for athletes and was set up by Jack Karavich in 2020 after developing the equipment working with students at LSU - hence the tiger association.

The company filed a lawsuit straight after Sun Day Red's launch in 2024 due to the similarity of the logos - with Woods' brand image containing 15 stripes on the tiger to represent his Major titles.

Subscribe to the Golf Monthly newsletter to stay up to date with all the latest tour news, equipment news, reviews, head-to-heads and buyer’s guides from our team of experienced experts.

Sun Day Red claims that Tigeraire "sought to deliberately manufacture a costly trademark dispute to secure a big payday" according to the written ruling from the court.

Their point was dismissed by the ruling, but the wider issue still remains unresolved as Tigeraire's initial federal lawsuit has been on hold since 2024 and there's no word on whether it still wishes to proceed.

The one dissenting judge in the recent Californian court case did side with Woods, pointing out the potential damage that could be done to Sun Day Red if it eventually had to change its logo on all products already produced and in stores.

It's unlikely to get that far but the two companies have so far been unabe to reach a compromise so talks may be needed to avoid any more complications.

Woods has been flying in his build-up to his comeback according to those in the know, while he's also just signed up to build a new links course in Northern Ireland as his TGR Design business thrives - he'll hope Sun Day Red can continue to follow that success.

Paul Higham is a sports journalist with over 20 years of experience in covering most major sporting events for both Sky Sports and BBC Sport. He is currently freelance and covers the golf majors on the BBC Sport website. Highlights over the years include covering that epic Monday finish in the Ryder Cup at Celtic Manor and watching Rory McIlroy produce one of the most dominant Major wins at the 2011 US Open at Congressional. He also writes betting previews and still feels strangely proud of backing Danny Willett when he won the Masters in 2016 - Willett also praised his putting stroke during a media event before the Open at Hoylake. Favourite interviews he's conducted have been with McIlroy, Paul McGinley, Thomas Bjorn, Rickie Fowler and the enigma that is Victor Dubuisson. A big fan of watching any golf from any tour, sadly he spends more time writing about golf than playing these days with two young children, and as a big fair weather golfer claims playing in shorts is worth at least five shots. Being from Liverpool he loves the likes of Hoylake, Birkdale and the stretch of tracks along England's Golf Coast, but would say his favourite courses played are Kingsbarns and Portrush.

title: MJ Daffue: DP World Tour player vows to 'kick butt' in battle with brain tumour after HotelPlanner Tour promotion
article_text:
DP World Tour player MJ Daffue has vowed to ‘kick butt and be ready to go soon’, having been forced to miss the start of the season after being diagnosed with a brain tumour.

Daffue won twice on the HotelPlanner Tour this season and finished fifth in the Road to Mallorca rankings, securing his DP World Tour card, before being hospitalised earlier this month for an infection that unearthed further health issues.

The 37-year-old has since revealed two tumours were found, including one benign on the liver, with Daffue now undergoing treatment to address the one found in his brain.

In a statement on his Instagram, Daffue said: "It's taken a while to post anything about this year because of the difficult time the past two weeks has been. This year has been incredible and we have been so blessed with good golf.

"Unfortunately, I ended up in the hospital with an infection about 10 days ago and after lots of tests they could not find the source. However they did find a tumour on my brain and my liver.

"Many more tests later, it was established that the one on my liver is benign, so we are very grateful. Unfortunately, the one on my brain is still a mystery.

"I am currently on strong medication to see if we can attack the legion on the brain but I am struggling a bit physically. I am in great spirits, and the care team and neurosurgeon has a perfect plan.

"I feel very confident that this is something that I will also kick butt and be ready to go soon. I appreciate all the messages so far and can't wait to be fully healthy and attacking the top of the leaderboards again soon."

Daffue previously held the halfway lead at the 2022 US Open, won by Matt Fitzpatrick, then graduated from the PGA Tour from the Korn Ferry Tour later that season.

He struggled for form over the following years and entered 2026 outside the world's top 800, only to post three top-10s on the DP World Tour and impress on the HotelPlanner Tour.

"I started the year with little to no ranking on the HotelPlanner Tour or the DP World Tour, but I worked hard, played intensely and was able to notch up a couple of early wins," Daffue said earlier this month.

"That made it possible for me to also fight for a card through the DP World Tour non-members points list, where I came up just short. I was pleased to finish the season with third place at the HPT Grand Final in Mallorca, which meant I finished fifth on the rankings.

"Starting the year with no ranking meant I had to take every playing opportunity I got. This meant it was hard to plan a schedule and so I spent weeks on the road, away from family and friends, which was hard.

"Most importantly, thanks to my wife for the love and being my rock - I can't be anything without you. So I'm super proud to come through the other side and it all be worthwhile."

title: MJ Daffue undergoing treatment on brain tumour following DP World Tour promotion
article_text:
South African golfer MJ Daffue has revealed he is undergoing treatment on a brain tumour, weeks after earning promotion to the DP World Tour.

The 37-year-old, who earned his first professional victory on the HotelPlanner Tour at the NTT Data Pro-Am on home soil in February 2026 and won the DP World PGTI Open a month later, took to his Instagram to share that he was hospitalised earlier this month, shortly after the Grand Final.

title: Faldo urges LIV stars to 'chip in' for unpaid firms
article_text:
Sir Nick Faldo has suggested, external those who financially benefited from LIV Golf should "chip in and take care of" businesses owed money by the Saudi-backed tour.

His comments have been welcomed by UK companies still waiting to be paid.

A BBC Sport investigation found that LIV paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while bills from suppliers were already overdue.

Faldo - arguably Britain's greatest golfer - said the controversial breakaway tour risked "ruining the small businesses that help make their events possible".

"British suppliers who cleaned venues and kept events running are still owed hundreds of thousands of pounds," added the six-time major winner.

"Maybe if those on and off the golf course feel they were overcompensated for their worth, they should chip in and take care of this matter."

Since the investigation was published, more firms have contacted us about money they are owed by LIV.

They include sports communications company Soapbox, which works with the likes of Anthony Joshua and Luke Littler and is owed tens of thousands of pounds.

"I'm incredibly grateful to Sir Nick Faldo for speaking out," said Krissi Foskett, whose cleaning company BD365 Clean is £75,225 out of pocket.

"For the last couple of months I've felt powerless. Having someone of his standing recognise the injustice of what's happening to businesses like ours genuinely means a lot.

"Sir Nick's suggestion that those who have benefited financially could contribute towards paying the outstanding suppliers is something I wholeheartedly welcome."

LIV Golf has not responded to requests for comment on the original investigation or Faldo's remarks.

In August, chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped the tour would be able to pay its suppliers.

"What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed.

"I come from a family of entrepreneurs, a family of small business entrepreneurs and know the challenge."

Faldo's one-time on-course rival, Greg Norman, was chief executive of LIV Golf until last year.

Court filings show the Australian received $9.4m (£7.2m) in settlement and bonus payments in September 2025.

His successor, O'Neil, received a retention bonus of $6.4m (£4.9m) in June this year.

In September, Norman told The Real Deal with Bob Philion podcast that he was proud of bringing private equity into the sport.

"In a period of basically 2021 to now, close to $8bn (£6.1bn) has been brought into the game of golf," he said.

Responding to those comments, Faldo told BBC Sport: "Eight billion dollars is 8,000 million dollars. If that is a full six years, that is approximately $3.6m (£2.8m) a day.

"Before LIV filed for bankruptcy, seven executives received $15.6m (£11.9m) in retention payments, with further bonuses also paid.

"Now they risk ruining the small businesses that help make their events possible."

BBC Sport has contacted Norman for a response.

Companies still owed money include Global Infusion Group, which provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event and is awaiting £321,671 - which was due on 7 August.

Public records also list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere, a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.

Just $2m (£1.5m) has been proposed so far by LIV's Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure whether they will receive anything at all.

"I've spent months questioning myself, feeling ashamed that our financial difficulties might be perceived as poor management," said Foskett.

"When I look at the billions poured into LIV Golf and the millions reportedly paid to executives, whilst I was personally climbing in and out of skips to meet their zero-waste policy, I've come to realise that I'm not the one who should feel ashamed.

"We didn't invest in LIV Golf. We didn't gamble on its success. We simply went to work.

"Scott O'Neil talks about understanding small businesses. Sir Nick Faldo is standing up for them. Right now, I know whose words mean more to me."

title: Sandy Scott makes strong start in first DP World Tour outing since 2023
article_text:
Sandy Scott marked his first DP World Tour start in more than three years with an eye-catching opening effort in the BMW Australian PGA Championship in Sydney.

The Nairn man carded a four-under-par 68 at The Lakes Golf Club in Sydney to sit handily-placed after the opening round of the 2027 DP World Tour schedule.

Starting at the tenth, Scott burst out of the blocks with back-to-back birdies before adding further gains at the 14th and 16th to be out in 33.

The world No 92 dropped his only shot of the day at par-4 third before getting that back with a fifth birdie of the round at the par-5 eighth.

The effort left Scott, who is gearing up to play on the PGA Tour next year, sitting in a tie for 11th as home player Haydn Barron set the pace with an eight-under-par 64.

Scott, a two-time winner on the Korn Ferry Tour in the US earlier this year, is making just his eighth DP World Tour appearance this week.

He played as an amateur in the 2017 Genesis Scottish Open at Dundonald Links before his next one was in the 2020 US Open at Winged Foot.

Then, in 2023, the former Texas Tech player teed up in the Hero Indian Open, Magical Kenya Open, Made in Himmerland, ISPS HANDA World Invitational and Alfred Dunhill Links Championship.

In his first appearance since becoming a new dad, Connor Syme carded a two-under-par 70 in Sydney to sit joint-26th heading into the second circuit.

The 2025 KLM Open champion, who hadn’t played since the Open de Espana in the middle of October, opened with nine straight pars before mixing birdies at the 11th, 14th and 17th with a bogey at the par-4 16th on the back nine.

On his return to the main tour after regaining a card through the HotelPlanner Tour last season, Marc Warren had to settle for a one-over 71 and sits alongside compatriot David Law in joint-93rd.

Also facing a battle to make the cut is new card holder Ryan Lumsden, who mixed four birdies with two double bogeys and three bogeys on a colourful card as he signed for 75.

Barron, who held a DP World Tour card in 2024 and has most recently plied his trade on the HotelPlanner Tour, signed for nine birdies and one bogey to lead by a shot from Kiwi Kazuma Kobori and American MJ Daffue.

Defending champion David Puig is handily-placed on three under, with 2022 Open champion Cam Smith and former world No 1 Adam Scott both sitting on one under.

title: How every former LIV Golf player performed in round one of the Australian PGA Championship
Rory McIlroy named Men’s Professional of the Year by Irish Golf Writers’ Association
Haydn Barron dominates day one in Sydney
article_text:
Haydn Barron carded the lowest round of his DP World Tour career to open up a two-shot lead as the 2027 Race to Dubai got under way on day one of the BMW Australian PGA Championship.

Alex Noren got the season started with the opening tee shot at 06.55 at The Lakes Golf Club but it was the man who went off just 25 minutes later who stole the headlines.

Barron carded nine birdies and a single bogey in a 64 that got him to eight under, two shots clear of Kiwi Kazuma Kobori and American MJ Maguire.

Barron claimed his first ranking win earlier this season on the PGA Tour of Australasia to finish fourth on its Order of Merit and then missed out at Qualifying School, the route via which he had earned a maiden DP World Tour campaign in 2023.

He finished 180th on the Race to Dubai that season and 80th in his first full campaign on the HotelPlanner Tour in 2026 as he looked to find his way back to golf's global Tour.

A win this week will take care of all that and he could do it with a little help from a friend as he has fellow professional Dimitrios Papadatos on the bag this week.

Papadatos had a top ten at this very event in 2025 and Barron revealed his fellow Australian has been a huge help through both his caddying and his friendship.

"Unreal, helped so much," he said. "I always say to people, I think I perform my best when I've just got someone out there to chat a bit of crap to, and he's definitely very good at doing that.

"He was a bit slow on a couple of numbers. I had to get there and then kind of coach him through how I got the additions to meet the number that I got to. But hopefully it'll be better for that tomorrow."

He added: "It was a good round. It was one of those ones that just kind of flowed, I guess. I never felt like I was really on fire, just all of a sudden, I was four under, and then all of a sudden, I was eight under. So yeah, I’m really pleased with the round.

"The confidence has been high enough. I've been playing well for kind of 12, 18 months now. It's just a matter of kind of putting four rounds together at a big event like this one. So, yeah, it's a good start and I'm looking forward to the rest of the week.

"They're very different sides. I was kind of cautious of that, after I'd finished nine. I was thinking, you know, it's completely different out the back, just especially with the wind kind of picking up a little bit on the turn as well. I’ve probably got to drive it. There's probably a couple more tough driving holes in the back nine, especially with the cross breezes. I was happy with the way that I drove my ball.

"It's one of those events start we look forward to all year. I’ve spent the last six months playing HotelPlanner Tour over in Europe, and you know, kind of always just trying to make sure I'm in my best condition for Q School and the Aussie PGA and the Aussie Open. The minute these events finished, you look forward to them for another 12 months. It's nice to have had a good start and be in this position."

Barron birdied his opener and then added a hat-trick of gains from the sixth to turn in 31. Three more gains in four holes from the 11th had him flying and while he dropped a shot on the 15th, he bounced back with two birdies.

The Aussie carded nine birdies and sign for a round of 64 (-8) to kickstart his week in Sydney.#AusPGA pic.twitter.com/YWtMgoiB1i

Kobori had a breakout rookie season in 2025 as he made the DP World Tour Championship and after not quite hitting those heights last term will be looking for a fast start close to home.

The 25-year-old started on the tenth and made three birdies on the back nine, adding another four and a single dropped shot on his way home.

Maguire, who has been an Asian Tour regular for the last four seasons, made four birdies in five holes from the 11th to surge up the leaderboard late in the day.

HotelPlanner Tour graduate Lars van der Vight holed a long putt on the last to sign for a 67 and sit three shots off the lead alongside Chinese pair Wenyi Ding and Ashun Wu, German Nicolai von Dellingshausen, home favourite Cam Davis, Canadian Sudarshan Yellamaraju and American Michael La Sasso.

Min Woo Lee, Daniel Hillier and Tapio Pulkkanen were among the group at four under, one clear of defending champion David Puig.

title: Smith, Niemann, Herbert: LIV's collapse could reshape the Presidents Cup
article_text:
The end of LIV has handed the Internationals back some of their best players for the 2028 Presidents Cup, and Australia may be the place the tide finally turns.

- The 2028 Presidents Cup at Kingston Heath could see LIV defectors Cam Smith, Joaquin Niemann and Lucas Herbert eligible again for the Internationals after LIV's demise.

- Captain Geoff Ogilvy's home-soil team will be bolstered by the likes of Ryan Fox, Dan Hillier and potentially Jason Day, Min Woo Lee and a 13th appearance from Adam Scott.

- Corey Conners believes Australia offers the Internationals' best chance yet to end the US's 11-straight Presidents Cup winning streak after their narrow Medinah loss.

Adam Scott at Kingston Heath in a 13th team, with Cam Smith, Joaquin Niemann and Lucas Herbert as his allies, all on captain Geoff Ogilvy's home turf.

That looms as the new scenario for the International team that went within one horror Sunday showing of ending the US dominance of the Presidents Cup at Medinah Country Club.

The advent of LIV did more to hurt the Internationals than the Americans in terms of loss of players, a point conceded and highlighted by Ogilvy, who took over the captaincy of an outfit that outplayed expectations and defied lopsided world rankings to lead the event into the final day in Chicago in September.

A lack of stone-cold winners and some nervous rookies, however, proved the difference in the Sunday singles, as the home team, feeling the pinch of increased criticism having also lost the Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black the year before, stormed over the top to claim an 11th straight win.

Turning the tables has proved difficult in the last two encounters, when LIV seized Smith, Niemann, Herbert and Marc Leishman, along with a bunch of eligible South African stars such as major champions Charl Schwartzel and Louis Oosthuizen.

New Zealander Ryan Fox elevated himself during that time and, after taking out the 2026 Open Championship, made his Presidents Cup debut at Medinah, with countryman Dan Hillier now also locked in as a PGA Tour player and someone for Ogilvy, who has yet to commit to captaining in 2028, to potentially turn to.

But it's the possible presence of Smith, who took down Justin Thomas in the Sunday singles in his lone appearance at Royal Melbourne in 2019, as well as Herbert, holder of the equal low round in major championship history after his 62 at Royal Birkdale this year, and Niemann, regarded as a top-10 player in the world who won nine individual LIV titles and also has an affinity with Australia, having won the 2024 Australian Open, that looms as key now.

Even Mexican stars Abraham Ancer, another Australian Open winner, and Carlos Ortiz are now eligible after LIV's demise, creating even more cause for excitement about what could happen in 2028.

Niemann and Ortiz will get an early look at Kingston Heath too in next week's Australian Open, and Smith's enthusiasm to get back into the Presidents Cup was obvious when he was asked this week, although he conceded he has a lot to do to make it happen.

"Yeah, for sure. I've only played one President's Cup and it was at Royal Melbourne, so just down the street. So yeah, Kingston Heath's a great venue. I'd love to be a part of that team," he said.

"But there's a lot of good stuff that has to happen between now and then to get on that team."

The opposition also get access to Bryson DeChambeau, but from am American standpoint he, and possibly major champ Dustin Johnson present as two of few former LIV player with selection credentials.

Canadian Corey Conners, who is in Australia for both the PGA and the Open after being part of the losing International team at Medinah, was adamant the Internationals were getting "closer and closer" and lauded the impact Ogilvy in particular had.

"Geoff did an amazing job captaining the team, bringing us all together, giving us something to play for," he said, having played under three different captains in three losing outings.

"All my experiences on the Presidents Cup, teams have been amazing, feels like a family.

"We played some good golf early in the week in Chicago to put ourselves in a great position, but getting over that line is obviously very challenging and I think we'd love to have another go at Sunday.

"Me personally, and I'm sure a lot of the guys will be working hard to try and make the team for Kingston Heath in a couple years. Playing in the US is tricky … and I would think I'd be a lot more comfortable playing in Australia as well. A lot more fans behind us."

Conners said that if the Internationals were going to end the US dominance, Australia, with Australians in the team including, potentially, Scott, Smith, Herbert, Min Woo Lee and maybe Jason Day, who missed 2026 through injury, and with Ogilvy at the helm, could be the place.

"I think if there's anywhere, I think Australia's… talking with some of the players I know excited to feel the warmth of the crowd, the people cheering us on here," he said.

"Obviously lots of avid golf fans and passionate fans of sport and similar to Canada in that sense, I think.

"I think you look how close we've been the last four Presidents Cups and maybe even more, but really legitimate chances to win and it was ours for the taking a couple of those times. I think it's just a matter of time before we finally get it done. I know the group's really motivated and I certainly am."

title: The longevity advantage: How PGA Tour, Cleveland Clinic are helping players stay competitive longer
article_text:
The PGA Tour Performance Truck presented by Cleveland Clinic helps players stay healthy at every career stage.

Editor’s note: This is Part 3 in a three-part series from the PGA Tour and Cleveland Clinic offering a behind-the-scenes look at today’s modern approach to player health and performance. This series explores what players can access inside the PGA Tour Performance Truck presented by Cleveland Clinic, how Cleveland Clinic experts use testing and insights to identify potential issues before they become injuries and how a comprehensive approach to health can help players stay competitive longer.

Longevity in professional golf isn't built overnight. For some players, it starts with the habits they establish as young professionals. For others, it means adapting to the physical demands of a career that can span decades. And increasingly, the conversation extends beyond how long a player can compete to how well he can live long after his playing days are over.

As today's Tour players become stronger and faster, the physical demands of the game continue to evolve. The challenge is learning how to sustain those gains without sacrificing long-term health.

Corey Hug, a Tour physical therapist, has seen the difference in the athletes coming onto Tour today.

“These new guys come in like Ferraris, but if you take care of (your body), it's going to be fine,” Hug said. “If you don't take care of it, you're going to get away with it for a while and then things start to break down. You want to stay ahead of it.”

For Tom Hospel, M.D., the PGA Tour’s chief medical advisor, that evolution reflects a broader shift in how players approach their careers.

“If you look at maybe the prototypical golfer 30 years ago and compare that to what the golfer looks like today, it's night and day,” Hospel said. “There is a huge focus on performance and overall health and wellness, and that includes recovery.”

Through the PGA Tour Performance Truck presented by Cleveland Clinic, players have access to medical screening, health assessments and performance and recovery resources at Tour events. The partnership is designed to support players at different stages of their careers, helping them understand their health today while making decisions that could influence their future.

For Michael Dakkak, D.O., a primary care and sports and exercise medicine physician with Cleveland Clinic, one of the biggest opportunities is helping players recognize that longevity isn't something to think about only when problems arise.

“We're seeing players peak earlier in their careers than they had in the past, with arguably more surgeries and more issues coming up earlier in their careers,” Dakkak said. “Because they're swinging the club so much harder. … But we’ve not been able to say: ‘Here's how you've moved over the course of your career,’ and I think having that longitudinal piece is going to be key to be able to predict things.”

That perspective is particularly important for younger players, who may feel healthy and see little reason to prioritize preventive care.

“Even the 23-year-olds, they think: ‘Oh, I'm healthy. I'm good. Nothing's going on,’” Dakkak said. “But if we dive further into that, it’s more about how do we keep you available on the course, walking on the course, not walking into our clinics?”

Tamanna Singh, M.D., a sports cardiologist and director of the Sports Cardiology Center and Stress ECG Lab at Cleveland Clinic, believes younger generations have an opportunity to use technology and health information to their advantage.

“I think a lot of people in our generation have been able to grow alongside technology, especially smart data and technology,” Singh said. “And I think that they're really good at taking advantage of that information. With the Tour’s partnership with Cleveland Clinic, players are able to have a team who's really helping them navigate that information.”

But the most meaningful gains aren't always found in the numbers. Singh points to the everyday decisions that help athletes stay healthy and prepared.

“The people who are really thriving are the ones who are making sure that, in those in-between moments, they are staying on top of nutrition, sleep, stress management, all of those things that are those ‘one percenters’ that can lead to a win,” Singh said.

Those habits, established early, can become the foundation for a longer and healthier career.

What works for a young professional may look different for a player who has spent 15 or 20 years competing at the highest level. As careers progress, maintaining performance often means understanding how the body changes and adjusting accordingly.

Hospel sees an interesting exchange between generations on Tour. Younger players are learning from veterans who have sustained their careers, while established players are navigating a game that continues to reward athleticism and power.

“The younger guys also look at how the older guys have been on Tour for a while and wonder what is their secret? What are the habits that they form? What is it that they're doing pre-round, mid-round, post-round in order to have a long healthy life and career on Tour?” Hospel said.

Hug sees the value of those routines in players who have made their health and fitness a long-term commitment.

“A lot of guys that have been playing out here well into their 40s, … they've been really good because they've been doing (their) program for 20 years, and so they're able to say, ‘Hey, I know what I need to do. I know I need to reset myself every day,’” Hug noted. “The guys that have been out here 20 years in their 40s, potentially approaching Champions Tour, there's still a lot of golf left.”

title: Casandra Alexander: Ladies European Tour Order of Merit winner on 'holes in the system' for players to earn LPGA cards
article_text:
Ladies European Tour Order of Merit winner Casandra Alexander has called for more pathways to be introduced to avoid players being ‘stuck’ in the same way she was to secure her LPGA Tour card.

Alexander is inside the world's top 30, has won three times on the Ladies European Tour this season and wrapped up the Order of Merit title with two events to spare, yet still needed to negotiate Final Qualifying to secure her LPGA Tour card for next season.

The South African has been a dominant force on the LET this season, posting five runner-up finishes before following KPMG Women's Irish Open victory with further wins at the Buccellati Ladies Italian Open and Wistron Ladies Open.

PGA Tour membership is offered in the men's game via the DP World Tour's Race to Dubai rankings, with the top 10 - not already exempt - earning their card this season, whereas top LET performers still need to earn LPGA cards via their Q-Series.

"It's definitely a little disappointing," Alexander admitted to Sky Sports. "There's not one person to blame - there's structures in place and I think it just shows the holes in the structure that we need to change.

"There's a lot that goes into it, but it was also a proving point for me this year, to get my world ranking as high as possible. I was hoping to break into the top 20 and go 'really, guys, are we still going to say there's only one way to get a card and that's Q-School?'

"We need to fix the system and we need to work together, because we want the best players in the world playing against the best players in the world and all having that opportunity."

Alexander enters the season-ending Andalucía Costa del Sol Open de Espana without a practice round having safely negotiated LPGA Qualifying, finishing Monday, where a final-round 64 helped secure her card on the American circuit next season.

"I'm not saying we need to hand out [LPGA] cards, but there surely has to be more than one pathway to earn it?" Alexander added. "I don't think the point of it is to say, 'oh, look at this, it's absolute rubbish', which it is, it's going, 'cool, but how do we do better?'

"I'm sure I wouldn't have the same attitude if I didn't get my card. I went there, I got my card, but how do we do better for the next people coming through? Because this isn't going to sustain itself - you're going to lose great players over this.

"A lot say the top three or top five on the LET Order of Merit should get cards - that's not necessarily how it starts. I think the conversation starts around 'how do I play my way into LPGA events, into gaining points and into potentially getting a full card?'

"It also shows that we need to be line-up with world ranking points because I don't understand how I was 23rd in the world and could play every major but couldn't play a general LPGA Tour event - that shows another hole in the system.

"We need to have a 'top 100 in the world' spot for any LPGA event. We have that on the LET and that would have given me opportunity to play eight or nine LPGA events this year. I hope someone else doesn't get stuck in the same situation I did in the future."

Alexander was keen to taper expectations heading into the season finale, given she only arrived in Spain the day before the tournament and without her luggage, although she is keen to enjoy the experience and celebrate an impressive season.

"I felt a little lighter leaving Alabama with the [LPGA Tour] card in my hands," Alexander admitted. "We're just coming in this week to have fun. We'll give it our best and I think it's important to show face as winner of the Order of Merit at the final event - that shows a lot of character.

"I'd love to be at home celebrating but, at the same time, it's going to be a fun week. There's the award ceremony afterwards and I think now I can take it all in. We've got a lot to do and a lot to plan [for 2027], and it's very exciting.

"It has been a really big, successful year. A lot learned and I have a great team around me that I can be thankful for, for all these achievements. It's a bit surreal, but still so much I want to do."

title: Brooks Koepka swipes Bryson DeChambeau over match fail: 'Didn't hole a putt the entire time'
article_text:
Before the rise of LIV Golf, Brooks Koepka and Bryson DeChambeau had one of the best (and most contentious) rivalries in pro golf.

The clashes between the major champions were not restricted to the golf course.

After Koepka followed DeChambeau to LIV, though, the former rivals seemed to transform into partners, at least publicly.

Now that LIV Golf is no more, however, the feud between the two stars is ratcheting up again.

Last month, Koepka zinged DeChambeau during a podcast appearance, saying Bryson “lives in his own world.”

On Tuesday, Koepka was at it again, taking another swipe at the two-time U.S. Open winner during a press conference for the upcoming Skins Game.

Koepka is prepping to take part in the second edition of the reborn Skins Game (known as the Farmers Insurance Skins Game) the day after Thanksgiving.

But in a press conference previewing the Black Friday match, Koepka got to talking about another pro-golf exhibition from the recent past: the 2024 Crypto.com Showdown at Shadow Creek. That event pitted Koepka and DeChambeau, who were LIV Golf pros at the time, against PGA Tour stars Rory McIlroy and Scottie Scheffler.

McIlroy and Scheffler handily beat Koepka and DeChambeau, earning about $5 million each in crypto tokens. Brooks and Bryson walked away with nothing.

During his press conference ahead of this week’s Skins Game, Koepka was asked about his experience at the Showdown. In his response, he blamed the loss on Bryson’s poor putting.

“Since I did not win, my teammate didn’t hole a putt the entire time, so I did not receive any of that,” Koepka said, taking a jab at DeChambeau.

He then said that it’s “great” that the Skins Game is “individual” instead of a team event like the Showdown, where he “didn’t get to choose” his teammate.

“Which is great because it’s an individual thing this time. So I’m more excited about that, but it’ll be fun,” Koepka said.

The comments come just weeks after Koepka joined the “Dan on Golf” podcast and threw more shade DeChambeau’s way.

DeChambeau famously complained that Rory McIlroy did not speak with him when they were paired together during the final round of the 2025 Masters.

Koepka had a unique explanation for McIlroy’s silent treatment, blaming it on DeChambeau.

“Well, I mean, [DeChambeau] lives in his own world. I mean, I don’t think many people want to talk to him regardless,” Koepka said.

So when will we next get to see Koepka and DeChambeau tee it up against each other? It might be a while. Koepka will be playing the PGA Tour next year, after rejoining ahead the 2026 season. DeChambeau, on the other hand, will play the DP World Tour for most of 2027. So, unless DeChambeau gets offered an accelerated path back to the PGA Tour, we won’t seem them in the same field until the 2027 Masters.

Koepka will face off against Justin Thomas, Wyndham Clark and Jackson Koivun in the Farmers Insurance Skins Game on Friday, Nov. 27.

title: Brooks Koepka rule improves pro's PGA Tour status for 2027
article_text:
Max McGreevy had just emptied the tank on the final day of the PGA Tour season. After a year in which he made 19 of 31 cuts but failed to produce any stellar results, the 31-year-old had needed to put together a good final round at the RSM Classic to give himself a chance at retaining some semblance of PGA Tour status.

But an even-par 70 at Sea Island left McGreevy tied for 10th. It was his best finish of the season but one that didn’t seem like it was going to be good enough to nudge him inside the top 125 to keep conditional status on the PGA Tour. When McGreevy walked off the course, he was bouncing between No. 126 and 127 in the FedEx Cup Fall standings. Those few spots are a huge difference — between getting 15-20 PGA Tour starts, as Lanto Griffin did in 2026 (17 starts) after finishing 125th last year, or largely plying your trade on the Korn Ferry Tour, as Frankie Capan III (only six PGA Tour starts), who finished 127th in 2025, did this year.

After the final round of his season, McGreevy spoke with the press about life on the bubble and how, after a subpar season, he was willing to face the repercussions for his below-average play.

“Just think your life can kind of change any week that you get out here, so as well as you can play and get every opportunity that you can get next year,” McGreevy said. “Unfortunately, I’m not going to finish where I wanted to at the end of the year, but hopefully get a couple starts, and if that’s the case, then hopefully I can take advantage when that happens. If I’ve got to go play more on the Korn Ferry Tour, golf is golf, life is life. We’ll go forward from here and yeah, try to keep moving up.”

An hour or so later, Marco Penge won a four-way playoff to end the season and finalize the rankings. There sat McGreevy at 126, seemingly one spot off the mark. In the end, though, he landed precisely where he needed. A one-year wrinkle due to the return of Brooks Koepka meant that McGreevy’s T10 finish at the RSM and No. 126 place in the FedEx Fall rankings was good enough to sneak into the conditional 111-125 category.

When Koepka returned from LIV Golf in January via the “Returning Members Program,” the PGA Tour wanted to make sure that his reintegration did not hurt its current members. As part of the return agreement, the Tour added two players to the field each time Koepka teed it up. The Tour also did not want Koepka’s return to affect another player’s ranking or eligibility in 2027, so they added a stipulation that any player who finished behind Koepka in the final rankings would move up one spot in the standings. The five-time major champion finished the year at No. 108 in the FedEx Cup Fall. That meant that Jason Day, who battled an injury in 2026, moved up from 111 to 110, which will give him conditional status in a category that doesn’t reshuffle; Day could also use a career money exemption in 2027.

Koepka’s return also meant that McGreevy, who finished 126th, will move up to 125th and, in 2027, be able to play out of that conditional category, which is subject to reshuffle.

That one spot can be the difference between a season grinding on the KFT vs. getting a decent chunk of starts on the PGA Tour. McGreevy’s T10 finish at the RSM put him two points ahead of Joel Dahmen for the final spot in the 111-125 category. That’s a one-shot difference between dropping back down and facing an uphill climb or holding on. McGreevy’s 70 on a windy Monday at Sea Island was good enough for him to finish three strokes better than Dahmen and one spot ahead in the final FedEx Cup rankings. With Koepka’s help, McGreevy barely held on instead of having to deal with a harsh reality of pro golf.

“If anything, as I’ve gotten older, I’m playing older, which I don’t necessarily think is a great suit for me,” McGreevy said of what he learned from a down 2026. “Ten years playing now, I think I have enough scar tissue to know when to take advantage and when to not. I’ve watched the young kids out here, and they’re just, they go 24/7 type of thing. I think I played a little bit more reserved than I probably should have all year. I made a lot of cuts, which is good for me; I’m usually pretty streaky. I just think I took my foot off the gas pedal a little too much this year and hopefully we can learn from that and just kind of move forward with it.”

Koepka’s return and two-point advantage over Dahmen gave McGreevy a professional lifeline in 2027. It’s up to him to make the most of it.
