LIV Golf profane domain names freed up following tour’s demise
article_text:
A tranche of domain names, including livgolfmyass.com, livgolfsucks.com and terroristgolfleague.com, bought up by LIV Golf to prevent critics creating insulting websites could now become available following the company’s liquidation.

The revelation shows how sensitive LIV Golf chiefs were when the controversial league, backed by billions from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, launched in 2022. LIV Golf collapsed after PIF withdrew funding in April.

This column recently revealed that executives were paid millions of pounds before the league filed for bankruptcy, while unsecured creditors, including a UK charity that uses sport to change the lives of vulnerable young people, are not expected to receive a penny back. The Change Foundation, based in Surrey, is owed £22,200.

Executives had hoped a rescue package led by BC Partners would save the league, but the private equity firm walked away due to concerns over the lack of elite players prepared to participate in “LIV 2.0”.

It may be music to the ears of detractors who may – or, indeed, may not – have tried to set up critical websites, only to discover LIV Golf had beaten them to it. Also among the 874 domain names LIV officials bought to keep them out of the hands of naysayers were bloodmoneygolf.com, corruptgolf.com and livgolfracist.com.

LIV Golf did not respond to a request for comment.

The London Stadium has been given the green light to host mega-fights after Newham Council indicated it would grant planning permission to increase its capacity for boxing events.

This column revealed in October that London Stadium bosses wanted restrictions relaxed to allow it to rival Wembley for blockbuster fights and help offset losses from anchor tenant West Ham’s relegation to the Championship.

As part of a wider planning application, officials requested that boxing be classified as a unique one-off event rather than a sport, which limits capacity to 60,000. Newham Council has now resolved to grant permission, subject to final sign-off on the planning agreement.

The stadium has become a £19m-per-year burden on taxpayers since West Ham were relegated from the Premier League in the summer but boxing could help soften the blow.

Anthony Joshua’s upcoming fight against Tyson Fury at the 80,000-seater Principality Stadium is expected to generate more than £20m. Under new terms, a fight night at the London Stadium could accommodate up to 85,000 fans if it is selected in one of eight slots for maximum capacity, while regular events would still be able to sell 80,000 tickets.

The council has requested that London Stadium officials make reasonable efforts to give 100 tickets to local residents.

Newcastle United are still spending money on determining whether to expand St James’ Park or build a new home three years into the project and despite being forced to sell many of their best players in the summer, City AM can reveal.

Sources with knowledge of the situation say both stadium options remain under active consideration. Building a new 65,000-seater ground from scratch at Leazes Park, a Grade II-listed site adjacent to St James’ Park and owned by Newcastle City Council, would be expected to cost around £1.5bn.

Expanding the existing stadium from 52,700 to 60,000 would be a considerably cheaper option at around £500m. The club continues to consult external advisers as it assesses the best course of action.

Newcastle were forced to sell key players in the summer, generating around £240m through the sales of Anthony Gordon to Barcelona, Sandro Tonali to Spurs and Bruno Guimaraes to Arsenal.

When Brighton and Hove Albion owner Tony Bloom makes a prediction, he rarely gets it wrong. Now the man who built a fortune by beating the odds through his data-driven betting operation, Starlizard, has predicted that Brighton will qualify for the Champions League.

It would be easy to get carried away with Brighton’s flying start to this season. They have emerged as surprise early challengers at the top of the table, outscoring everyone and beating Arsenal and Manchester City, two of the dominant forces of recent years.

But Bloom is a cool calculator, so a prediction made during an Overcoming Multiple Sclerosis event at the Amex Stadium recently should not be taken lightly.

Aston Villa are considering scrapping their in-house TV channel’s £30 annual subscription fee for season-ticket holders and members after it was pointed out by fans that rival clubs offer a similar service for free.

Currently, season-ticket holders, who pay upwards of £700 per season, receive access to Aston Villa TV at half price. But Villa, who are set to earn at least £50m from playing in this season’s Champions League, will discuss removing the 58p-per-week charge for season-ticket holders and members next year.

title: 'Very Australian': Smith wants Ripper GC name to LIV on
article_text:
Long-time skipper of the all-Australian Ripper GC team, Cameron Smith has outlined his plans for the popular branding following LIV Golf's demise.

Strident junior golf supporter Cameron Smith hopes the Ripper GC name will live on despite the collapse of LIV Golf.

Captain of the all-Australian outfit for four years, Ripper GC drew huge galleries while winning three team events on the Saudi-backed circuit plus the 2024 season-ending championship.

But while the team is no more after LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy, Smith would love to see the Ripper GC brand endure in some shape or form, likely in a junior development capacity.

The 33-year-old former British Open champ established the Cameron Smith Scholarship in 2016 and also contributes to the broader Australian Golf Foundation.

"I would love it too because I think it's a great name and and it's grown a lot of legs the last few years," Smith said ahead of Thursday's first round of the Australian PGA Championship in Sydney.

"It's very Australian and I think a lot of kids have a lot of great memories with it as well.

"But we don't really know where that stands with everything going on, but for sure I would love to do something."

While the likes of LIV peers Phil Mickelson, Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm have polarised during golf's great divide, Smith's reputation as a fan favourite has remained relatively intact.

He proved the Pied Piper of the fairways annually at LIV Golf Adelaide and said he always felt the love of golf galleries around the world and especially at home.

"I've always had great support in Australia," the three-time Australian PGA Championship winner said.

"I'm so thankful for that. (It) was a difficult time for me, so I'm thankful for particularly Adelaide and Australia in general for getting behind me."

His name already etched on the Kirkwood Cup three times, Smith enters this week No.171 in the world after being denied the chance to earn ranking points for years playing in the LIV league.

But after missing six straight cuts at the majors, getting into Sunday contention and finishing seventh at this year's US PGA Championship under new swing coach Claude Harmon had renewed his belief.

"It's been a while since I've been able to perform in a major. I'd just started working with Claude probably two or three weeks before that," Smith said.

"Whenever you make a change, you're really unsure if it was the right decision or not, and that just hit the nail on the head and got the ball rolling and we've been doing the right stuff and the game's felt really good.

"We just need the putts to go in and the results to follow."

title: USGA, R&A provide significant update to golf equipment changes: Answering 5 burning questions
article_text:
The latest twist in the golf ball rollback saga has arrived.

Late last week, the USGA and R&A quietly released a “notice to manufacturers” indicating they have identified two paths to limit distance gains in professional golf and are targeting approval of those changes in time for the start of the new PGA Tour schedule in 2028.

At first glance, the changes outlined by the governing bodies aim to limit distance gains for pro players with the driver and golf ball, but appear to fall short of the distance drops targeted by the golf ball rollback standard initially pursued back in 2023.

But let’s hold on for a second. If you’re a golfer with a normal degree of exposure to governing body minutiae, you’ve probably got no idea what I just said. So let’s get you the goods without the headache in Q&A form.

The USGA and R&A have been looking to curb distance in pro golf for years … but as it turns out, it’s pretty hard to curb distance! Players hate it. Club companies hate it. Regular golfers hate it. The governing bodies don’t even seem to like it.

In fact, it might be said that curbing distance in golf is a lot like eating chard — if it’s so good for you, why does it taste like that?!

The USGA and R&A are unusual in that they are self-aware enough to recognize their chard-iness. They have tried very hard to find a solution to the distance problem that will satisfy everyone or, at least, annoy everyone the least.

First the USGA and R&A pitched a golf ball rollback that would only affect Tour pros. That led to a mutiny. Then, in late 2023, they pitched a rollback for all golfers, pro and recreational. Another mutiny. THEN, in early 2026, they announced a sudden agreement with the PGA Tour to work toward new solutions to curb distance while pushing back the deadline for the rollback-for-all to 2030. No mutiny this time … well, except for all the regular golfers who understood a rollback was necessary to preserve the sport in its purest form. Among that crew? Yep, you guessed it: Mutiny.

Now we have last week’s announcement, which appears to show plans to cut back driver AND golf ball distance … but by what sounds like a smaller margin than the original all-golfer rollback. That’s good news if you didn’t want to lose 15 yards every time you teed off at Bethpage with your buddies. It’s good news if you’re a pro golfer who didn’t want to lose 15 yards at the Masters. And it’s good news if you’re the USGA and R&A and you know you’ve gotta do something to stop the steady creep of distance increases.

2. What is the change the USGA and R&A are promoting?

Basically, they want to make their equipment tests harder to pass. Right now, the equipment companies have wiggle room in how their golf balls and drivers get tested. When the ball is tested, it has a three-yard buffer where it can travel beyond the legal threshold without “failing” the test. When the driver face is tested, it has an 18-microsecond buffer where it can spring beyond the legal threshold without “failing” the test.

Under the changes proposed by the USGA and R&A, which would go into effect in 2028, the driver face and golf ball would be required to stay at or below the legal limit. Considering those changes aren’t aspiring to lessen the distance standard — just test it more stringently — it seems unlikely the changes will produce a considerable distance loss with the golf ball or driver. But a better fence would theoretically defend against continued increases in ball flight.

3. Would *my* golf ball travel shorter if this rule passed?

Nope! These changes are “model local rules,” which means they would be enforced only for the pro tours that choose to adopt them, and not for everyday Joes like you and me.

4. What about that other golf ball rollback? The one you guys have spent three years telling me about?

The rollback for all golfers is still scheduled to go into effect in 2030. That plan, which would change the testing thresholds to lower driving distance for everybody, in theory losing as much as 15 yards off the drives of the longest-hitters, is still ongoing. But it might be on the brink of changing. The 2030 test conditions are being revised, and last week’s notice committed to giving “updated test conditions” to club manufacturers. Earlier this year, GOLF reported that the change could involve the shape of drivers and/or the thickness of the driver face.

At a time of considerable change in professional golf, new distance standards represent the most seismic shift to the game as golfers know it. For years, elite-level players have been gaining distance off the tee — changes driven at least in part by advancements in golf ball and driver technology. These changes, which have changed the way pro golf is played at the highest levels, have concerned the governing bodies responsible for upholding golf’s traditions, its courses and itssense of competitive fairness.

Beyond the historical record and scoring implications of players hitting the ball farther than ever, these changes have threatened many of golf’s most historic tournament hosts. Changes to driving distance have forced many of the world’s best golf courses to undergo costly expansions in order to host high-level men’s events, and have all but eliminated many other historic courses from consideration for such events.

title: Brooks Koepka Aims Yet Another Dig At Bryson DeChambeau
article_text:
Brooks Koepka just can't help himself when it comes to aiming jibes at Bryson DeChambeau, with his latest coming in the build-up to The Skins Game this Friday.

The Farmers Insurance Skins Game will be shown on Prime Video on Friday 27 November with Koepka taking on Justin Thomas, Wyndham Clark and Jackson Koivun at Atlantic Fields Golf Club in Florida.

But although there will be plenty of trash talking between the foursome as they battle it out for $4m - the biggest dig landed in the pre-event press conference was aimed at someone not even taking part.

Koepka was asked about a similar event - The Showdown in 2024 - when he teamed up with DeChambeau in a sign their long-running fued had been squashed.

However, reflecting on that heavy defeat to Rory McIlroy and Scottie Scheffler in the $10m crypto contest Koepka again showed there's no love lost between the two.

"Since I did not win, my teammate didn't hole a putt the entire time, so I did not receive any of that," said Koepka.

"Which is great because it's an individual thing this time. So I'm more excited about that, but it'll be fun."

Subscribe to the Golf Monthly newsletter to stay up to date with all the latest tour news, equipment news, reviews, head-to-heads and buyer’s guides from our team of experienced experts.

Koepka was also keen to point out he "didn't get to choose" his teammate for that last head-to-head contest.

From fierce enemies to teammates in both the Ryder Cup and then The Showdown, Koepka and DeChambeau were never best buddies but their relationship seemed cordial until recently.

Asked about DeChambeau's experience alongside McIlroy during the final round of the 2025 Masters, Koepka was equally as scathing.

DeChambeau complained about McIlroy blanking him at Augusta National as he finally ended his search for a Green Jacket - with the Northern Irishman wondering why he'd be so chatty when history was on the line.

It was clear which side Koepka was on when he said "I don't think many people want to talk to him regardless" in reference to DeChambeau.

Koepka also said DeChambeau "lives in his own world" during that interview with Skratch's Dan Rapaport and it's clear the two personalties simply don't mix.

DeChambeau is seen more on YouTube than the golf course these days, but if the two ever tee it up in the same event again it'll be one to watch.

Paul Higham is a sports journalist with over 20 years of experience in covering most major sporting events for both Sky Sports and BBC Sport. He is currently freelance and covers the golf majors on the BBC Sport website. Highlights over the years include covering that epic Monday finish in the Ryder Cup at Celtic Manor and watching Rory McIlroy produce one of the most dominant Major wins at the 2011 US Open at Congressional. He also writes betting previews and still feels strangely proud of backing Danny Willett when he won the Masters in 2016 - Willett also praised his putting stroke during a media event before the Open at Hoylake. Favourite interviews he's conducted have been with McIlroy, Paul McGinley, Thomas Bjorn, Rickie Fowler and the enigma that is Victor Dubuisson. A big fan of watching any golf from any tour, sadly he spends more time writing about golf than playing these days with two young children, and as a big fair weather golfer claims playing in shorts is worth at least five shots. Being from Liverpool he loves the likes of Hoylake, Birkdale and the stretch of tracks along England's Golf Coast, but would say his favourite courses played are Kingsbarns and Portrush.

title: Marco Penge puts difficult year behind him to secure PGA tour card
article_text:
Marco Penge pulled off one of the most dramatic escapes in recent golf history at the 2026 RSM Classic. Entering the final week of the season ranked 120th in the FedEx Cup standings, the 28-year-old Englishman needed a top-four finish just to keep his PGA Tour card.

He delivered far more, birdieing the 72nd hole to force a four-man playoff before draining a clutch birdie putt on the first extra hole to claim his maiden PGA Tour title and a two-year exemption. Here is the story behind the resilient golfer who appears to thrive when his back is against the wall.

1. An accidental start at the driving range

Born in Crawley, England, in May 1998, Penge discovered golf purely by chance at age five. His mother bought his father, Angelo, a cheap set of clubs for his 40th birthday to help him relax. Angelo took young Marco along to the Pease Pottage driving range, where the boy picked up a club and immediately striped the ball straight down the fairway.

That natural talent led to formal lessons at Mannings Heath Golf Club and eventually a standout amateur career that was highlighted by winning the 2015 Scottish Amateur Stroke Play Championship.

After turning professional in 2017, Penge took the long road to the top. He honed his craft on the third-tier PGA EuroPro Tour, earning his first pro victory at the 2019 Irish Masters.

He then graduated to the Challenge Tour, where his breakthrough arrived in 2023. That season, Penge won twice, including the season-ending Rolex Challenge Tour Grand Final, to top the Order of Merit and secure his promotion to the DP World Tour.

Penge has been refreshingly open about living with ADHD, explaining that the condition can easily cause him to overthink on the course. Rather than viewing it as a limitation, he has worked closely with his team to build strict routines and mental structures that prevent overstimulation.

Penge credits understanding his own mind as a massive factor in his professional success, noting that the golf course is actually where he feels most at ease.

Penge’s career hit a major roadblock in December 2024 when the DP World Tour handed him a three-month suspension and a £2,000 fine for breaching its integrity program.

An investigation revealed he had placed small bets on golf tournaments between 2022 and 2024. Although he never wagered on himself or events he was competing in, the ban sidelined him heading into 2025. Penge owned up to the mistake, attributing it to a misunderstanding of the rules.

Returning from suspension in February 2025, Penge played with a chip on his shoulder and enjoyed a career-defining year. He captured his maiden DP World Tour title at the Hainan Classic in April, followed by victories at the Danish Golf Championship and the Spanish Open.

He finished second in the Race to Dubai rankings, climbed inside the world’s top 30, reportedly turned down a massive LIV Golf offer, and earned his 2026 PGA Tour card.

Penge’s 2026 transition to the United States tested his resilience to the limit. Following a move to Florida with his wife, Sophie, the couple endured a terrifying stretch when their newborn son spent four weeks in neonatal intensive care.

Simultaneously, Penge battled a debilitating viral illness and vertigo that forced him to step away from golf for six weeks after the PGA Championship.

Slumping in the standings, he arrived at Sea Island needing a miracle – but he delivered in style to turn a season of personal and physical adversity into a career-defining triumph.

title: David Puig’s Ryder Cup Dream Hits A New Road After LIV Collapse
article_text:
David Puig has made his target crystal clear. The 24-year-old Spaniard wants a spot on Europe's 2027 Ryder Cup team. He told reporters that making the squad is "another dream of mine since I was young." This isn't just a side note for the young star. Puig sees the team at Adare Manor next September as his main goal now that the LIV Golf landscape has shifted.

Puig is starting his full season on the DP World Tour this week. He defends his Australian PGA Championship title in Sydney. The field includes major winners like Cameron Smith and Adam Scott. Puig knows the path is steep. In 2026, his world ranking peaked at 56th. A top-20 result was also achieved at the US PGA Championship. But the road to the Ryder Cup requires consistency. "Playing in a Ryder Cup would be amazing," Puig added, according to Golfmagic. "I'll try my best. Hopefully it's enough to be on the team in September."

While Puig chases a player spot, others have already lost their shot at leadership. Ian Poulter confessed he would give up his Ryder Cup captaincy hopes for Europe. He discussed the price he paid after joining the Saudi-backed league. Poulter said he accepted the possibility of losing the role. "Yes, I've sacrificed being a Ryder Cup captain," he said. He understood the rules when he made his move.

The financial hit was real too. The DP World Tour reportedly fined Poulter approximately $1.1 million. The tour confirmed in June 2026 that Poulter settled the debt. That payment did not restore his eligibility for future leadership. The rules state that players who resign their membership cannot become captains. Poulter even compared his earnings to a potential $10 million a year deal with Sky Sports. He described his career earnings as "an obscene amount of money." The message is simple. You cannot play both sides and expect a leadership role.

Puig's situation offers a stark contrast to the LIV fallout. The 24-year-old has not resigned his membership. During the tour's three-week Opening Swing, Puig intends to compete two times. He will skip the Australian Open to play the Nedbank Golf Challenge in South Africa. He wants to see more of the world while building his case for Europe. "It's hard when two great tournaments combine with each other," Puig explained. "It was definitely a tough decision, but I'm looking forward to playing here this week and there next week." His focus remains on the game. "But it starts in weeks like this where playing good golf definitely matters."

European captain Luke Donald is seeking a historic third consecutive victory. The team will face the United States at Adare Manor.

title: Scottie Scheffler, Cameron Young and Wyndham Clark headline PGA Tour Player of the Year award nominees
article_text:
The PGA Tour on Tuesday announced nominees for the two major awards it hands out each year, Player of the Year and Rookie of the Year. Scottie Scheffler, Cameron Young, Wyndham Clark, Matt Fitzpatrick and Chris Gotterup make up the five-man race for the Jack Nicklaus Award, while Alex Fitzpatrick, Ben James, Kristoffer Reitan, Jackson Koivun and Marco Penge are among those vying for the Arnold Palmer Award.

Scheffler has become familiar with getting his hands on the Jack Nicklaus Award in recent years. The world No. 1 joined Tiger Woods as the only golfer to claim the title three years in a row when he secured the honor in 2024. After winning it again in 2025, Scheffler can join Woods again as the only players to ever win it five times in a row. The 15-time major champion won the award five straight seasons from 1999-2003 and three straight from 2005-07.

In 2024, Scheffler became the third golfer to be named Player of the Year three times in his career, joining Woods (11 times) and Rory McIlroy (three). He surpassed McIlroy -- who is not nominated for the award for the first time since the 2020-21 season -- by winning the award again last season.

Scheffler's campaign for a fifth straight Nicklaus award appeared in doubt as he went through the PGA Tour regular season with just one victory. He made up for lost time in the postseason by winning the St. Jude Championship and the Tour Championship for his second career FedEx Cup crown.

The 30-year-old finished inside the top 10 in three of the four major championships, had the lowest scoring average on the PGA Tour and missed only one cut this season.

Scheffler's season was one highlighted by consistency, while Clark's was one of memorable achievements. Clark fired a final-round 60 at The CJ Cup Byron Nelson for the first win of his year before grabbing his second career U.S. Open victory at Shinnecock Hills, with Scheffler by his side on that fateful Sunday.

The wins by Scheffler in the FedEx Cup Playoffs sandwiched a win by Clark at the BMW Championship as he got the better of McIlroy in St. Louis.

Clark and Scheffler's win total of three were matched by both Fitzpatrick and Gotterup. Fitzpatrick won the Valspar Championship before edging out Scheffler in a playoff at the RBC Heritage the week after the Masters. The Englishman was not done, however, and scored the biggest win of his season at the Zurich Classic where he helped secure a PGA Tour card for his little brother Alex.

Meanwhile, Gotterup got off to the hottest start with wins at the Sony Open and the WM Phoenix Open. The big-hitting right hander added another at the John Deere Classic to polish off a transformational season.

Gotterup paired up nicely with Young at the Presidents Cup, one year after Young notched his first win on the PGA Tour. He added to his tally in 2026 with wins at The Players Championship and the Cadillac Championship amid a stretch in the spring where he was the hottest player in the world.

The Rookie of the Year race will be just as compelling given the influx of young talent on the PGA Tour in 2026. Five players are in the running with four of them notching victories, including Penge who claimed the season-finale at the RSM Classic to maintain his playing privileges on the PGA Tour in a season where he dealt with injury.

His fellow Englishman, Fitzpatrick, won the Zurich Classic with his brother, Matt, and went onto collect six top-10 finishes in a limited run on the PGA Tour. One of those finishes came at the Truist Championship where Fitzpatrick fell just short to Reitan, who captured the biggest win of any rookie on the PGA Tour in 2026.

Reitan won the signature event at Quail Hollow Club and also had a top-10 finish at The Memorial Tournament. While the Europeans fared well early in the season, the Americans brought the excitement late with Koivun winning the 3M Open in his third start as a professional. The highly touted amateur got the better of Scheffler at TPC Twin Cities to earn the trophy.

Koivun did not have enough rounds to qualify for a scoring average on the PGA Tour in 2026 where James ranks second only to Scheffler. The No. 1 from PGA Tour University started his career at the Canadian Open and has not looked back as all five of his top-10 finishes also doubled as top-five efforts, including his playoff loss at the World Wide Technology Championship.

The honors will be awarded through a voting process, including PGA Tour members who played in at least 15 official FedEx Cup events during the 2026 season. Voting closes on Friday, Dec. 4 with winners announced at a later date.

title: LIV Golf Creditors Threaten Chapter 7 Liquidation Over $2M Offer
article_text:
LIV Golf’s Chapter 11 bankruptcy case in New Jersey is at risk of being converted to a Chapter 7 liquidation process.

The official committee of unsecured creditors in LIV’s case does not support the current wind-down plan, which is offering just $2 million for general recovery claims. “At present, the plan only benefits the debtors’ current and former directors and officers and the Public Investment Fund of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” the committee wrote in a statement and reservation of rights filed Monday evening.

A Dec. 4 deadline has been set by the creditors and LIV to reach a deal or “immediately move to convert these cases to Chapter 7 and conduct an orderly liquidation of their assets.” In the meantime, settlement negotiations between all parties are underway. The creditors committee did not object to conditional approval of LIV’s revised disclosure statement and wind-down plan, which was granted by Judge Michael Kaplan on Tuesday morning.

If the case converts from Chapter 11 to Chapter 7, LIV’s management team would lose control of proceedings, and a court-appointed trustee would take control of the bankruptcy estate. The Saudi PIF is LIV’s largest creditor, since the nearly $500 million of funding it gave the league to finish the 2026 season came in the form of a secured loan. The sovereign wealth fund put up $49.6 million in debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing to fund the bankruptcy process, and is funding the $2 million being offered to unsecured creditors.

A major concern for the committee is the $2 million being offered for unsecured claims. “At consideration levels that low, the committee believes that unsecured creditors would be better off in a Chapter 7 liquidation,” its statement read. “Given the strength of the claims against PIF and the size of the claims pool—which may exceed $1 billion—any consensual resolution of these cases will require PIF to considerably increase the PIF cash consideration.” The committee also noted that the $2 million pot “would yield materially less than one cent on the dollar in terms of recoveries for general unsecured creditors.”

LIV is arguing Chapter 7 would be worse for everyone involved, though. “We think it would destroy value for all parties,” Matthew Williams, one of LIV’s attorneys from Gibson Dunn, said during Tuesday’s virtual hearing. “The debtors believe that Chapter 7 will leave unsecured creditors worse off, and we don’t think it serves the PIF either.”

The creditors committee is represented by New York–based law firm Willkie Farr & Gallagher and New Jersey–based Fox Rothschild. “We look forward to the continued good-faith negotiations amongst all the parties,” Willkie partner Jim Burbage said Tuesday. “And while there is a lot of wood to chop before we get to a deal, we do remain optimistic that the parties will be able to reach a consensual resolution in the relatively near term.”

Creditors in LIV’s case range from the league’s former star players like Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau—who are owed millions of dollars—to various other contractors and vendors who say they remain unpaid for work they provided for LIV.

Dec. 3 is the next scheduled hearing date in LIV’s bankruptcy case.

title: Tiger Woods 'Melting' The Ball Ahead Of Comeback As Justin Thomas Splits With Caddie: This Week In Golf
article_text:
This Week In Golf: Our regular look at key stories in the game you might have missed as well as other important details you need to know from around the world.

The PGA Tour season has drawn to a conclusion following Marco Penge's dramatic RSM Classic victory, so what's going on this week?

We have a new and highly anticipated DP World Tour season starting Down Under, the return of the Skins Game, the Ladies European Tour finale and much more.

In this edition of This Week In Golf, we'll take you through the latest news and give you all the info you need to know about what's going on in the professional golf world this week. Starting with a certain Tiger Woods...

Tiger Woods is set to return to PGA Tour action next week for the first time since the 2024 Open, having had further injury setbacks and then another high profile car accident in recent times.

The Californian golfing great, now 50, will tee it up in the Hero World Challenge in The Bahamas and progress reports are already filtering out in the media.

No Laying Up's Tron Carter said Woods is reportedly 'melting' the golf ball and carrying bunkers at 320-325 yards per someone who played with him recently.

Subscribe to the Golf Monthly newsletter to stay up to date with all the latest tour news, equipment news, reviews, head-to-heads and buyer’s guides from our team of experienced experts.

It's getting fans excited for the great man's return, and a further podcast report came from Barstool Sports' Fore Play Pod, which said Woods has been doing three-mile incline walks each day to get his fitness back to where it needs to be.

Woods will almost certainly play in the PNC Championship next month, too, where he and son Charlie will be the headline team. All being well, we can expect to see him play a number of times on the main tour, Champions Tour and the Majors next year.

Justin Thomas has split with caddie Matt Minister after nearly two seasons together.

The two-time PGA Champion will have a friend, Brad Gehl, on the bag for the upcoming Skins Game and is hiring Michael Cromie for the 2027 season according to Golfweek.

Thomas and Minister did not manage a victory together since teaming up at the 2024 Masters, as the American won the RBC Heritage with stand-in looper Joe Greiner.

Cromie previously worked with Chris Kirk and also stepped in for Ted Scott at the 2025 BMW Championship and went on to win alongside Scottie Scheffler - bagging $360,000 in the process.

One of the most highly anticipated DP World Tour seasons in recent memory gets underway this week in Sydney at the BMW Australian PGA Championship.

David Puig defends his title in a strong field featuring the likes of Cameron Smith, Adam Scott, Min Woo Lee, Lucas Herbert and a number of DPWT regulars and ex-LIV Golfers.

The Lakes GC hosts the event ahead of next week's Australian Open at Kingston Heath, which will feature Rory McIlroy.

It will be the first of 42 tournaments on the schedule in 24 countries, which includes the return of the Singapore Open, Portugal Open and Hong Kong Open. This week's tournament features an AUD $2.5m prize fund.

The former Ripper GC captain is one of nine players to have agreed DPWT sponsor invite deals for 2027, and he admitted his goal is to make his way back to the PGA Tour.

"I guess that's the path. That's where I want to be now for sure," Smith told the Australian Associated Press.

"DP's given us a chance to kind of fulfil that. We'll see how that goes. There's plenty of good players out there and plenty of other guys that want to do the same thing, so it's going to be difficult.

"But for sure that's where I want to play.

"I think given what they've told me, I pretty much need to win this year to get membership.

"It's all still very blurry to me at the moment. There are a lot of rules, but we'll have a few opportunities, and like I said, I've always managed to play pretty good down here, so why not start it off with a good one?"

The Skins Game returns for its second edition since re-launching last year, where Wyndham Clark, Brooks Koepka, Justin Thomas and Jackson Koivun will compete for a share of the $4m purse.

The event takes place on Black Friday, November 27 at 9am ET, and will stream live on Prime Video. Atlantic Fields Club in Hobe Sound, Florida will be the stage, with Andrew Catalon, Colt Knost and Dan Rapaport on the mics.

The rules have changed from last year's 'Reverse Purse' back to a standard format where all four players start at $0. As per usual skins rules, each hole carries a dollar value and tied holes roll over to raise the stakes.

La Cala Resort hosts the Andalucía Costa del Sol Open de España this week on the Ladies European Tour.

The season finale sees a 75-woman field competing over 72-holes with no cut, where the winner will earn €105,000 from the €700,000 prize fund.

Casandra Alexander has already secured the Order of Merit but the Rookie of the Year title is still on the line.

Alexander headlines the field alongside Mimi Rhodes, Anne van Dam, Anna Huang and Ana Peláez Triviño.

title: PGA Tour reveals nominees for 2026 Jack Nicklaus Award, Arnold Palmer Award
article_text:
PONTE VEDRA BEACH, Florida – The PGA Tour announced Tuesday nominees for the Jack Nicklaus Award (Player of the Year) and the Arnold Palmer Award (Rookie of the Year) for the 2026 season as finalized by the PGA Tour Player Directors and members of the Player Advisory Council (PAC).

Five players are nominated for the Jack Nicklaus Award as the 2026 PGA Tour Player of the Year (alphabetically): Wyndham Clark, Matt Fitzpatrick, Chris Gotterup, Scottie Scheffler and Cameron Young. The five nominees for the Arnold Palmer Award as the 2026 PGA Tour Rookie of the Year are Alex Fitzpatrick, Ben James, Jackson Koivun, Marco Penge and Kristoffer Reitan.

The Player of the Year and Rookie of the Year awards are determined by a member vote, with PGA Tour members who played in at least 15 official tournaments during the 2026 season eligible to vote. The voting will close Friday, Dec. 4, at 5 p.m. ET, with the winners announced at a later date.

- Entered 25 events with wins (three) at THE CJ CUP Byron Nelson, U.S. Open and BMW Championship

- No. 5 in the Official World Golf Ranking and No. 21 in the FedExCup

- Ranked third on Tour in Putting Average (1.698) and eighth in Bounce Back Percentage (28.29%)

- No. 3 in the Official World Golf Ranking and No. 21 in the FedExCup

- Ranked inside the top 10 on Tour in SG: Approach the Green (10th/.605), SG: Around the Green (second/.494) and SG: Total (second/1.359)

- No. 7 in the Official World Golf Ranking and No. 4 in the FedExCup

- Ranked third on Tour in Driving Distance – All Drives (309.2)

- Entered 20 events with wins (three) at The American Express, FedEx St. Jude Championship and Tour Championship

- No. 1 in the Official World Golf Ranking and claimed the FedExCup title

- Winner of the Byron Nelson Award for Low Scoring Average (68.619)

- No. 4 in the Official World Golf Ranking and No. 11 in the FedExCup

- Ranked ninth on Tour in SG: Tee-to-Green (1.092) second in Round 2 Scoring Average (67.90)

- One of two rookies to qualify for the Tour Championship and finished No. 4 in the FedExCup

- Made 12 cuts in 14 starts and finished No. 53 in the FedExCup Fall standings

- Earned PGA Tour membership as the No. 1 player in the 2026 PGA Tour University Ranking

- Made 10 cuts in 12 starts and finished No. 67 in the FedExCup Fall standings

- Made 15 cuts in 22 starts and finished No. 64 in the FedExCup Fall standings

- One of two rookies to qualify for the Tour Championship and finished No. 25 in the FedExCup

A player’s rookie season is defined as the season in which he becomes a PGA Tour member and plays in 10 or more events as a member or finishes in the top 100 in the FedExCup standings or qualifies as a top 70 non-member, whichever occurs first. A new member who previously played in more than seven official PGA Tour money events as a professional in a prior season is not eligible for PGA Tour Rookie of the Year.

title: David Lipsky falls out of top 100, Marco Penge soars in during dramatic FedExCup Fall finale
article_text:
ST. SIMONS ISLAND, Ga. – The PGA Tour season ended with no shortage of drama.

For the second consecutive week, a Tour event needed a Monday finish, and this time, 72 holes weren't enough to crown a champion. The RSM Classic came down to the Tour's first four-man playoff since the 2015 Greenbrier Classic, with more than a tournament title hanging in the balance.

Players spent the final round moving in and out of the top 100 in the FedExCup Fall standings, fighting to secure full status for 2027. When the dust settled, only two players had crossed the all-important threshold.

Marco Penge delivered the biggest move, climbing from No. 120 to No. 64 after birdieing the first playoff hole to claim his maiden PGA Tour title. David Lipsky, meanwhile, fell from No. 97 to No. 102 after missing the cut, leaving him with conditional status for next season.

Then there was John Parry, who walked off the Seaside Course on Friday believing he had lost his card. Instead, he survived a weekend of leaderboard movement to finish at No. 100, claiming the final spot for full status in 2027.

Here's a closer look at the players who moved across the bubble and where other notable names finished in the FedExCup Fall finale.

- Marco Penge (FedExCup Fall No. 120, projected No. 64)

Penge arrived at Sea Island Golf Club needing at least a two-way tie for fourth to crack the top 100. He left with far more than a PGA Tour card.

Returning to the 18th for the first extra hole, Penge delivered another precise wedge shot and made birdie to secure his first PGA Tour victory. The win earned him an exemption through 2027, spots in The Players Championship, The Sentry and the PGA Championship, plus a spot in the Tour's inaugural season of the Championship Series in 2028.

For Penge, winning wasn't necessarily the objective when the week began. Keeping his card was.

"The start of this week, my goal was to get into the top 100, and then felt like it was so stressful day by day, shot by shot. (I was) just trying to make sure I didn't do anything stupid," Penge said. "I'm kind of prone to hitting a wild tee shot here and there, so I was trying to keep it on the straight and narrow."

He did just that, missing only one fairway during Monday's final round.

With his playing privileges on the line, Penge initially approached the day with caution. But as the round progressed and his position inside the top 100 became more secure, his focus shifted from protecting his card to chasing the trophy.

"I felt like once I got through maybe nine holes today, I felt that I was going to be OK," Penge said. "Maybe for 14 holes I thought, OK, I've got a chance where I can actually win this. Then I kind of changed my mindset all of a sudden and tried to birdie every hole coming in. Luckily, I just did enough to get into a playoff and got it over the line."

The victory was another defining moment for Penge, who had previously navigated a similar fight to retain his status on the DP World Tour. This time, he emerged with a title and renewed confidence in his ability to perform when the stakes are highest.

"I proved to myself I can do it under the most immense pressure," Penge said. "I always seem to play my best golf when my back's up against the wall. I've been through this before on the DP World Tour, keeping my card in the last event and dealing with adversity and coming back from health issues, all that stuff. So I knew I could do it, I just wasn't sure I ever had the game this week to be able to do it, and thankfully I did."

- David Lipsky (FedExCup Fall No. 97, projected No. 102)

Lipsky entered The RSM inside the top 100 but will have to settle for conditional status in 2027 after missing the cut by two shots at Sea Island. He made 15 cuts in 25 starts this season, highlighted by a runner-up finish at the Valspar Championship.

- John Parry (FedExCup Fall No. 96, projected No. 100)

Few players endured a more anxious weekend than Parry, whose missed cut left his future on Tour in the hands of others.

A three-putt on his final hole Friday at the Seaside Course brought the Englishman to tears, believing he had squandered his chance to retain full status. With no more golf left to play, all he could do was watch.

As the final two rounds unfolded, Parry's projected position fluctuated above and below the top-100 cutline. Ultimately, the results fell his way, leaving him at No. 100 and securing the final full-status spot for 2027.

The Belgian fell short of the top 100 but made a significant move toward securing playing opportunities for next season. Four rounds in the 60s (68-66-68-67) earned Dumont de Chassart a tie for seventh, his best finish of 2026, and lifted him inside the top 125 for conditional status in 2027.

Sea Island once again brought out the best in McGreevy, who followed last year's runner-up finish with a tie for 10th. But despite another strong showing, the 31-year-old Oklahoma native couldn't climb high enough in the standings to secure full status.

title: High Time: How Craig Kessler and his ‘scrappy’ team are putting LPGA back together
article_text:
NAPLES, Fla. – Craig Kessler is running out of time.

It’s Tuesday morning ahead of the LPGA’s season finale, the CME Group Tour Championship, and the second-year commissioner has less than 15 minutes until his 9 a.m. pro-am tee time, he’s yet to hit balls, and to top it all off, his cart is nowhere to be found. Not that Kessler is fretting, even with the first hole a few hundred yards away.

With one strap of his carry bag slung over his shoulder, he calmly strolls to the range, where he strikes about a dozen balls, mostly wedges, and then heads to the tee, still on foot.

Ironically enough, Kessler arrives to find his cart waiting for him, but less than a hole into Kessler’s round, he ditches it anyway to walk with his playing partners, which include LPGA veteran Jenny Shin and executives from Ford and American Express. Kessler later suggests to the group that maybe all pro-ams should be cart-less for the sake of better conversation. He’s not wrong.

Over the next several hours, the 41-year-old Kessler provides a masterclass in personability. The storytelling in the group is so good that Shin, on a few occasions, must remind her caddie he still has a job to do. When she and two of the amateurs pour in three 30-plus-footers on top of each other on the third green, Kessler quips, “Want to take the magnet out of the bottom of the cup now?”

As his first full season winds down, Kessler, the man, is already proving himself a force.

But what about Kessler, the leader? While the LPGA has some nice wins already in the Kessler era, its boss isn’t satisfied.

“I’m so proud of what the team has accomplished this year,” Kessler says. “I’m thrilled with the progress we’re making but clear-eyed about how much work we still have to do.”

A glass of red wine in hand, Kessler makes the rounds inside The Ritz-Carlton’s lobby bar on Wednesday night, conversing with his employees, sponsors and random guests who are probably shocked to be chatting with someone of Kessler’s standing.

Before that, Kessler had just spent a couple hours at a media reception, usually the type of function where execs can’t wait to dip, especially considering the day’s itinerary. Kessler started with a 9 a.m. state-of-the-tour press conference, then attended an LPGA Foundation board meeting before his 10-minute spot just after noontime on Golf Channel’s “Golf Central,” which is airing the first of five hours before a shot is even hit in the $11 million tournament. He has a few sit-downs as well. In between obligations, he catches up with his wife, high-school sweetheart Nicole, who offers words of encouragement.

By Thursday morning, Kessler is up early and in the hotel café, still energized and eager to chat.

It’s a stark contrast to Kessler’s predecessor, Molly Marcoux Samaan, who often struggled to work the room.

Under Samaan, the LPGA saw a significant increase in prize money. Major purses more than doubled. The winner’s check at the season-ending CME ballooned to $4 million. But the tour otherwise remained stagnant at best, losing viewership, sponsors and perhaps most importantly, the trust of the players. Operational and communication gaffes such as the shuttle crisis at the 2024 Solheim Cup only raised the temperature underneath Samaan’s hotseat, until Samaan resigned in December 2024, less than five years into her post.

The common opinion about Samaan is that she failed to inspire, both internally and externally.

“They say it takes a village, and I think their village is getting a little fractured,” Terry Duffy, CEO of CME Group, told Golfweek back in 2022 after not a single player attended a sponsor dinner the Tuesday evening of the season finale.

Kessler heard as much during his interview process.

“I probably talked to dozens of people … and the theme that kept surfacing was the importance of building trust,” Kessler said. “The organization certainly had some scar tissue, so building trust was priority No. 1, trust with the players, sponsors, staff.”

Before Kessler, then the COO of the PGA of America, signed his contract, he met one on one with a few of the LPGA’s biggest names, knowing he needed their buy-in. After more than 200 days on the road, the father of three boys has earned it.

“He’s always asking what we can do better but also what is going well,” said Hannah Green, one of the LPGA’s player directors. “He’s always enthusiastic about trying to make this place better, and perhaps we haven’t had that in the past. I think Mike [Whan, now CEO at the USGA] was a great leader. I never worked with Molly, but I feel like sometimes people get the short end of the stick and they’ve got nothing to really work with.”

Said fellow player director Lauren Coughlin: “Every time I hear him talk in any kind of big setting, I’m just very impressed by him. He’s great with people. He’s so smart. I just don’t know how he keeps it all in his head. It’s crazy sitting in a board meeting and he doesn’t even have like a ton of notes or anything.”

Added veteran Alison Lee: “It seems like he cares so much about every single player on this tour. … He does a really good job showing us that as well, so it makes us feel heard. It makes us feel like we can go to him whenever we want.”

title: LPGA Tour card blow for Gemma Dryburgh at end of Q-Series
article_text:
Gemma Dryburgh has lost her seat at the LPGA Tour’s top table for the first time since 2018 after having to settle for Epson Tour status at the end of the circuit’s Q-Series.

The Aberdonian, who landed a maiden victory in the TOTO Japan Classic in 2022, finished joint-47th in the five-round card battle at RJT Trail at Magnolia Grove in Mobile, Alabama.

The top 25 and ties secured Category 15 cards for the 2027 LPGA Tour season, with all the other players completing at least four rounds earning Epson Tour status.

Dryburgh, who played in the 2023 Solheim Cup in Spain, found herself involved in this year’s Q-Series after finishing 114th in the 2026 Race to CME Globe Ranking on the LPGA Tour.

In the same position in 2021, she finished T22 to hang on to her card for the main tour before going on to claim 45th spot on the money–list the following season then a career-best 41st in 2023.

She slipped to 70th last season and will now be bitterly disappointed to have ended her first year playing as a new mum on a low note.

South African Casandra Alexander, this year’s LET Order of Merit winner, was among a total of 27 players to secure LPGA Tour cards for next season.

Meanwhile, Lorna McClymont will go straight to the final stage in the upcoming LET Lalla Aicha Qualifying School in Morocco through finishing 18th in this season’s LET Access Series Order of Merit.

Hannah Darling, Louise Duncan, Gabrielle Macdonald, Taylor White, Laura Beveridge, Alison Muirhead, Kimberley Beveridge, Kirsty Mitchell and Summer Elliott all face First Stage tests on 10-12 December, also in Morocco.

title: These 8 big names just lost their PGA Tour card
article_text:
Marco Penge was 120th in the FedEx Cup rankings heading into one of the biggest weeks of his career at the RSM Classic. It seemed the Englishman was going to be among the most surprising names to lose their PGA Tour card.

But Penge has a habit of delivering when under the gun. Two years after salvaging his DP World Tour card with a gutsy finish in Korea, Penge not only did enough to keep his playing rights in America, but he claimed his first PGA Tour title.

After a ‘nightmare’ season derailed by personal health and family issues, Penge saved his best until last with a five-under 65 on the rain-delayed final day, forcing his way into a four-man playoff. He birdied the first extra playoff hole to win a $1.3million prize and, crucially, secure his place in the lucrative PGA Tour Championship Series from 2028.

There was another English success story, too. John Parry, who missed the cut after a disastrous three-putt on his closing hole, somehow clung on to the 100th and final card after an agonising weekend wait.

Only the top 100 golfers after the FedEx Cup Fall Series secured their full cards for next year, while the top 125 are given conditional status and starts into certain events.

But for every John Parry there was a story of woe and regret. Here are the notable and surprising names who have lost their PGA Tour card…

A brutal end to what was so nearly an uplifting start to his PGA Tour career. The likeable Dane made 18 cuts in 24 starts this year, but he slipped down the leaderboard at the RSM Classic on Monday and narrowly misses out on full playing rights.

It could have been so different for Li. He was part of the four-man playoff won by Penge and had chances to win the tournament. But he will now mix his time between the PGA Tour and the DP World Tour next season.

Horschel returned from hip surgery in May 2025 and played a full schedule, but graded his 31-event season an ‘F’. The former FedEx Cup champ was not all doom and gloom though as he still retains conditional status. “I know I’m going to get in quite a few events and I’ve got to be able to take advantage of those opportunities,” he said.

The 2025 European Ryder Cup player had a torrid run, withdrawing from both the Biltmore Championship and the Butterfield Bermuda Championship, while missing the cut at the Bank of Utah Championship. But it all looked entirely salvageable as Hojgaard held the lead at the RSM Classic. He headed into the final round needing a tie for third for survival, but only managed T5 as he stumbled to the finish line. He will still make some PGA Tour starts, but right now Hojgaard looks to be the most likely dispensable from the winning team at Bethpage as we approach another Ryder Cup year.

It seemed inconceivable that the 2009 US Open champion would lose his card, especially after the renaissance that saw him win twice in a matter of weeks three years ago. But the 47-year-old’s age caught up with him during an abject year where he failed to capitalize on his position in Signature Events.

The Full Swing star had a mini-revival after appearing overawed on the PGA Tour. The two-time Korn Ferry Tour winner had a horrific start to the season and two top-10 finishes in the fall came too late.

Before Jackson Koivun, Blades Brown and Ben James it was Luke Clanton who was supposed to be America’s next superstar. That of course could still transpire, but this was a year when the youngster went backwards. Clanton made transition to the top table look seamless as a college player, threatening the leaders numerous times as an amateur. But in the paid ranks he’s struggled only made half of his cuts this season.

Dahmen was in contention at Torrey Pines at the start of the season before he was blown away by Justin Rose. Back in February, it seemed the lovable American had something to build on. But it has been a struggle since for Dahmen, who only just missed out on conditional status via the top 125.

title: For sure I want to return to the PGA Tour, says ex-LIV Golf player Cameron Smith
article_text:
SYDNEY – Australian Cameron Smith has moved on from LIV Golf, is preparing for his invitation-only appearances on the DP World Tour and is already thinking about a return to the PGA Tour.

As the 2022 British Open champion prepared for the Australian PGA Championship starting on Nov 26 at The Lakes in Sydney, attention inevitably turned to his career goals and his steps toward a possible return to the PGA Tour.

“I guess that’s the path. That’s where I want to be now for sure,” the 33-year-old told the Australian Associated Press. “DP’s given us a chance to kind of fulfil that. We’ll see how that goes. There’s plenty of good players out there and plenty of other guys that want to do the same thing, so it’s going to be difficult.

“But for sure that’s where I want to play.”

Currently, the top 10 from the European tour’s “Race to Dubai” season points list qualify for the PGA Tour. To even have a chance at that, Smith needs to play more tournaments on the DP World Tour’s 2027 schedule.

He could do that by winning the co-sanctioned Australian PGA Championship for a fourth time or the Dec 3-6 Australian Open at Kingston Heath, which also features world No. 2 Rory McIlroy.

“I think given what they’ve told me, I pretty much need to win this year to get membership,” Smith said. “It’s all still very blurry to me at the moment. There’s a lot of rules, but we’ll have a few opportunities and like I said, I’ve always managed to play pretty good down here, so why not start it off with a good one?”

The PGA Tour board last week said it had “thoughtful discussions” about the future of players at LIV Golf but otherwise seemed to be in no hurry to decide if there is room for them next season.

CEO Brian Rolapp said the “returning member programme” that allowed Brooks Koepka to return to the PGA Tour in 2026 with financial penalties was not on the table.

Smith did not take up that one-time offer in January, which applied only to players who had won Majors or The Players Championship from 2022 till 2025.

So he is in a kind of limbo. LIV Golf, which lost the financial support of Saudi Arabia and filed for bankruptcy on Sept 8, told a bankruptcy court earlier in November it had abandoned plans for a new version of the league and had begun winding down its business.

“There was a lot of uncertainty and then in a way it was good to just like get the noise over and done with,” Smith said. “It was a big move to go to LIV at the start for sure, and I think everyone that was close to me and all my friends saw why I was doing it and why I made the decision.”

Former world No. 1 and 2013 Masters champion Adam Scott said he had no doubts about Smith fitting back in.

“Cam’s incredibly talented and he’ll adjust to his new environment,” the 46-year-old Australian said. “He’ll be just fine.” AP

title: Who's in, who's out? PGA Tour's playing status drama goes down to final putt
2026 LPGA Q-Series Final Qualifying final results: Prize money payout, leaderboard, who earned LPGA status
article_text:
The 2026 LPGA Final Qualifying final leaderboard is headed by winner Megha Ganne, with the American player winning the five-round marathon on the Robert Trent Jones Golf Trail at Magnolia Grove -- the Crossings Course and Falls Course -- in Alabama.

Ganne won the 90-hole event on 23-under total, good enough for a one-shot win over Shannon Tan and Julia Gregg.

In total, 27 players earned LPGA status for 2027. Players finishing in positions 1-25 and ties earned LPGA Tour status in Category 15, giving them entry into most full-field LPGA events. Players who finished outside that top 25 and ties have status on the Epson Tour in 2027 in Category C.

In the final round, which closed on Monday, four players moved from outside the top 25 and ties into the cutoff: Marie Madsen (T-34 to T-15), Maria Fassi (T-46 to T-23), Achiraya Sriwong (T-41 to T-23) and Da Yeon Lee (T-41 to T-23).

The cutoff to get an LPGA card for 2027 was 3-under 283 and better. A total of 114 players from a starting 114 completed the tournament.

Ganne won the $15,000 winner's share of the $150,000 purse.

Final Qualifying is a five-round competition with a cut after 72 holes. Magnolia Grove (Crossings and Falls Courses) hosted the entire event, with the Crossings holding the final round.

This is the latest iteration for Final Qualifying, which had been known as Q-Series and had replaced the third-and-final stage of LPGA Q-School. The final stage was previously eight rounds in the first four years, turning to six last year and a scheduled five for the last two years.

There was a cut after four rounds to the top 65 and ties to make it a little easier to get the field through the difficult final round to maintain status.

title: GB, French, German swimming bodies launch annual competition
article_text:
The governing bodies for swimming in Great Britain, France, and Germany have teamed up to launch a new annual international competition as they seek to modernise the sport and attract new audiences.

The 3 Nations Cup is a joint venture between Aquatics GB, the French Swimming Federation, and the German Swimming Federation and will debut in Manchester on March 14, 2027, before moving to Paris on March 21.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

The new annual series will feature 22 races over 90 minutes. Mixed relays sit alongside women’s and men’s 50m ‘skins’ races in butterfly, backstroke, and breaststroke. Six swimmers will start, with four advancing, and just two reaching the final round.

To add an element of engagement and interaction to the team contest, spectators will draw the swimming order for the mixed 4x200m freestyle relay.

Points will count across both legs, and the team at the top of the standings after Paris will take the 3 Nations Cup title and share the prize money.

Through the 3 Nations Cup, the three federations said they are “creating a fresh way for fans to experience elite swimming, and a new platform through which to engage audiences, broadcasters, and commercial partners.”

Drew Barrand, Aquatics GB CEO, said: “It is time for elite swimming competition to evolve. Together with our counterparts in France and Germany, we have created a series that puts the excitement of racing at its heart.

“We want fans to feel the pressure of every race. With elimination rounds, mixed relays and points carrying across two weekends, the 3 Nations Cup gives them a fast-paced team contest to get behind from the first start to the final touch.

“This is a shared venture and a shared ambition. Leading from the front means putting new ideas into action, and all three nations are bringing that commitment to the pool.”

Next month, the International Swimming League (ISL), the club-based professional series, will also be making its return.

The league's upcoming one-night relaunch event, the ISL All-Star Match, will take place at the London Aquatics Centre in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park on December 19.

The All-Star Match will see the world's fastest swimmers compete in a team-based, two-hour, head-to-head competition.

Stakeholders in the sport are increasingly looking to maintain annual interest in swimming outside the Olympics through frequent, short-form competitions.

For British swimming, the 3 Nations Cup opens a three-part season in 2027, ahead of the Aquatics GB Swimming Championships in London in April and the World Aquatics Championships in Budapest in July.

Live coverage is planned for both legs of the 3 Nations Cup, with broadcast details to follow.

Earlier this year, the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), the continent’s association of public-service broadcasters, expanded its partnership with Aquatics GB to boost the visibility of international events in the UK.

The expanded agreement will see an increase in the range of events available free-to-air (FTA) in the UK throughout the year, including swimming, diving, artistic swimming, and open water swimming, via the Eurovision Sport streaming service, which will be embedded within the Aquatics GB website.

title: Newcastle Jets Re-Sign Alka Power as Official Hydration Partner for 2026/27 Season
article_text:
The Newcastle Jets have re-signed Australian alkaline beverage brand Alka Power as the Official Hydration Partner across both the club’s A-League Men’s and A-League Women’s teams for the 2026/27 season.

The renewed agreement restores category exclusivity for the functional beverage supplier across the Hunter region franchise’s senior football programmes.

Founded in 2012, Alka Power distributes its high-pH alkaline water nationally across major supermarkets, independent grocers, and petrol and convenience retailers, leveraging elite domestic football partnerships to reinforce everyday health and cellular hydration positioning among active consumers.

Alka Power managing director, Steve Pettaras, highlighted the value of returning as exclusive hydration partner across both senior Jets squads for the 2026/27 campaign.

“Alka Power is again proud to return as the exclusive Hydration Partner of the Newcastle Jets men’s and women’s football teams.

“As a natural high pH alkaline hydration water, we know how important it is that players keep hydrated on a cellular level.

“That’s why Alka Power has been the number one alkaline water brand for well over a decade. Best of luck to all for the 2026/27 season,” Pettaras said.

Dual-Squad Category Exclusivity: Secures exclusive Official Hydration Partner status covering both the Newcastle Jets A-League Men’s and A-League Women’s programmes throughout the 2026/27 season.

High-Performance Product Supply: Supplies naturally high-pH alkaline hydration water to support player recovery and hydration management across domestic A-League and continental AFC Champions League Elite schedules.

National Retail Leverage: Connects on-field club visibility with Alka Power’s nationwide distribution footprint across major supermarkets, independent grocery chains, and convenience outlets.

title: Matt Fagerson to miss rest of 2026 as Townsend issues update on quartet
article_text:
Matt Fagerson will be miss the rest of 2026 but is expected to be fit for the Six Nations despite suffering a fractured jaw in the win over Japan last week.

Fagerson became the latest Scotland player ruled out of the Nations Championship finals weekend with the injury, picked up in the second half of the 67-5 win at Murrayfield last Saturday.

He joins Glasgow team-mates Sione Tuipulotu, Scott Cummings and Alex Craig on the sidelines, while Scotland are also without Jack Dempsey, Ben White, Pierre Schoeman, Jamie Ritchie, Fergus Burke and Elliot Millar Mills.

But head coach Gregor Townsend offered an optimistic outlook on Fagerson's condition.

"We've got good news that it doesn't require surgery, so the healing process will take what it takes, but we believe he'll be OK for Six Nations," the Scotland boss said at the media launch for the Nations Championship finals weekend in London.

Ritchie, meanwhile, has missed all of the autumn after picking up a knee injury on his home debut for Glasgow Warriors.

Townsend said: "He was going to be I think about two to three months at the time, so what was that long, so he'll be maybe another month.

"That was disappointing for Jamie, because obviously before camp as well, they played so well in those two games in basketball, but it's an opportunity for someone else.

"Liam [McConnell] obviously played really well the weekend. You're always gutted for the guys who get injured, but you see someone come into camp and take that opportunity, then that makes up for it from a sporting perspective."

And Townsend has confirmed that both Rory Darge, who assumed the captaincy against Australia in the absence of Tuipulotu, and prop Nathan McBeth are set to be fit to face Argentina on Sunday.

He said: "Nathan [McBeth] has trained fully, Rory's [Darge] trained fully, so they're both available, so we're in a better place than when I chatted to you guys after the Japan game."

Townsend was initially concerned about McBeth's injury, which could have left Scotland facing a shortage at loosehead prop with Schoeman and Jamie Bhatti also currently unavailable.

But the Scotland boss said scans had shown it was not as severe as first thought.

"With these high ankle sprains, you'd think syndesmosis is a common injury, but it wasn't that, and again he's trained fully, so when I left Murrayfield [to travel to London] they were doing scrummaging, and nobody's messaged me to say don't get through that."

title: AITA presidential election: Chintan Parekh vs Rohit Rajpal - two visions for Indian tennis
article_text:
NEW DELHI: The race for the All India Tennis Association (AITA) presidency pits Chintan Parekh's "Tennis First" motto against Rohit Rajpal's "The Next Serve," with both candidates promising to address Indian tennis' structural challenges.

While Parekh's pitch centres on governance reform, financial sustainability and expanding tennis beyond established centres; Rajpal has outlined a more programme-driven roadmap with specific proposals, timelines and targets. Their approaches differ on how to tackle key issues confronting Indian tennis.

Chintan Parekh wants to expand talent scouting beyond established centres, with a focus on underserved regions such as the North-East. His vision includes coaching pyramids and grooming young players for a stronger tennis ecosystem by 2030.

Rohit Rajpal proposes a state-wise development audit within 100 days, common talent-identification protocols, zonal camps, a central player database and low-cost talent scouting in underserved districts.

Chintan Parekh wants to take tennis to regions lacking infrastructure, particularly beyond metropolitan centres, and tap talent in remote and underserved areas.

Rohit Rajpal plans to expand national and zonal centres of excellence, partner state associations, develop infrastructure in the Northeast and hill regions, and explore a high-altitude training centre.

3. More tournaments at domestic and international level

Chintan Parekh focuses on strengthening AITA's finances to fund tennis development, but has not outlined specific targets for tournament expansion.

Rohit Rajpal wants to bring ATP and WTA events back to India, expand Challenger, ITF and junior tournaments, rotate events across zones, and build women's and senior circuits with at least 30 tournaments annually by 2030.

Chintan Parekh identifies better governance as the key pillar under his presidency. He promises transparent, player-centric governance and a clean-up of AITA's institutional structure. He wants the AITA Trust to be brought under the association's umbrella, its trustees restructured, and issues concerning AITA's relationship with Delhi Lawn Tennis Association (DLTA) resolved.

Rohit Rajpal proposes published accounts, budgets and fund utilisation, along with Athletes, Ethics and Dispute Resolution committees. He also promises transparent selection criteria, calendars and measurable progress reports.

5. How to make tennis financially viable

Chintan Parekh wants to build AITA's corpus to ₹200-250 crore over four years, tap CSR funding and create greater financial capacity to support budding players.

"Our vision is a very clean AITA with a focus on the players. Grassroots development is important so scholarships for talented children in rural areas(is one target).

Tennis is still considered an affluent sport, one for the elite. The first step is to clean it up (the corruption). The second step is to build the grassroots, then get the funding in, empower the state associations who empower the players,"

, who is the vice-presidential candidate in Parekh's team, had told select media after filing his nomination.

Rohit Rajpal proposes travel and tournament-entry assistance for professionals, a CSR-funded Players' Distress Fund and a feasibility study for a pension scheme for retired players.

Should AITA prioritize expanding tennis infrastructure in underserved regions?

Parekh's pitch is centred on institutional reform, financial strength and widening tennis' reach. Rajpal's manifesto offers a structured roadmap with programmes, timelines and measurable targets.

Both promise to address Indian tennis' longstanding challenges. The real test, however, will be turning those promises into tangible opportunities for players.
